scenes.heading: Why compliance is the centre of gravity
scenes.subheading: You are the bridge between your client and a layered system of UK regulators
scenes.narration: The UK has no single tax and companies office. Instead there are several regulators, each with its own powers, deadlines and penalties, and as an accountant you are the bridge between them and your client.

scenes.heading: What happens when you miss a deadline
scenes.narration: Missing a deadline triggers automatic penalties, often charged daily. Serious failures can lead to director disqualification, professional sanction, or even criminal prosecution.

items.label: Automatic penalties
items.detail: Triggered by a missed deadline, often on a daily basis

items.label: Disqualification or sanction
items.detail: Director disqualification or professional sanction

items.label: Criminal prosecution
items.detail: Possible for the most serious failures

scenes.heading: The three pillars of compliance
scenes.narration: Compliance rests on three pillars: keeping proper records, reporting them in the returns and accounts each regulator requires, and paying what is owed by the legally specified date.

items.label: Record-keeping
items.detail: Capture every transaction to HMRC and Companies Act standards

items.label: Reporting
items.detail: Turn records into statutory returns and accounts on time

items.label: Paying
items.detail: Settle Income Tax, Corporation Tax, VAT, NI and PAYE on time

scenes.heading: Bookkeeping serves the return
scenes.narration: Debits and credits exist to serve those pillars. A trial balance is not an end in itself; it feeds a CT600, an SA100 or a set of FRS 102 accounts.

items.label: Ledger entries
items.detail: Debits and credits recorded in the books

items.label: Trial balance
items.detail: The input, not the end product

items.label: Statutory output
items.detail: CT600, SA100 or FRS 102 accounts

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: From day one, test every ledger entry by asking where it will end up on the statutory return, and whether it is correctly classified for that purpose.

scenes.heading: HMRC: His Majesty's Revenue and Customs
scenes.subheading: What the UK tax authority does, how it is organised and how agents work with it
scenes.narration: HMRC was formed in 2005 by merging Inland Revenue and HM Customs and Excise. It is a non-ministerial department: Parliament sets tax law in the Taxes Acts, and HMRC administers it.

scenes.heading: What HMRC actually does
scenes.narration: HMRC collects Income Tax, through PAYE for employees and Self Assessment for others, plus Corporation Tax, VAT, National Insurance, Capital Gains Tax, Inheritance Tax, Stamp Duty Land Tax, and customs and excise.

items.label: Income Tax
items.detail: ITEPA 2003, ITTOIA 2005, ITA 2007; PAYE or SA

items.label: Business taxes
items.detail: Corporation Tax via CT600; VAT returns under MTD

items.label: NI and capital taxes
items.detail: NI Classes 1 to 4, CGT, IHT, SDLT in England and NI

items.label: Customs and excise
items.detail: Especially important post-Brexit for goods

scenes.heading: Key filing periods
scenes.narration: UK residential property disposals need a separate 60-day Capital Gains Tax return. The CT600 is due within 12 months of period end, and personal representatives file the IHT400 within 12 months of death.

items.label: CGT property return
items.detail: Separate to Self Assessment

items.label: Corporation Tax CT600
items.detail: From the end of the accounting period

items.label: Inheritance Tax IHT400
items.detail: From death, filed by personal representatives

scenes.heading: Wider roles and legal status
scenes.narration: HMRC also enforces the National Minimum Wage, still runs legacy tax credits, and supervises anti-money-laundering for unsupervised advisers. Its legal basis is the Commissioners for Revenue and Customs Act 2005.

items.label: Minimum Wage enforcement
items.detail: Investigates underpayment; can name and shame

items.label: Tax credits
items.detail: Phasing into Universal Credit; legacy still run

items.label: AML supervision
items.detail: For advisers without a professional body

items.label: CRCA 2005
items.detail: Officers act under the Commissioners' care, s.5

scenes.heading: Silos, post and agent access
scenes.narration: HMRC works in tax silos, each with its own helpline, portal and BX9 address. BX9 routes to central digital mail, so never post to Whitehall. Agents need Gateway, the old agent account and the Agent Services Account.

items.label: Pick the right silo
items.detail: SA, CT, VAT, PAYE, CIS or Agent Authorisation

items.label: Use the BX9 sub-code
items.detail: e.g. Self Assessment BX9 1AS, VAT BX9 1WR

items.label: Hold the right accounts
items.detail: ASA is mandatory for MTD VAT, MTD ITSA, TRS, CGT

items.label: Get authorised
items.detail: Form 64-8, or now usually ASA digital code

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: Parliament makes tax law and HMRC administers it, each tax has its own statute and silo, use BX9 addresses, and authorise agents digitally through the Agent Services Account where you can.

items.label: ASA for MTD and digital auth

scenes.heading: Companies House: The Registry
scenes.subheading: What it records, what is changing under ECCTA, and the deadlines that matter
scenes.narration: Companies House is the UK registrar of companies, an executive agency of the Department for Business and Trade. It is a registry, not a regulator, recording what is filed rather than checking it is true.

scenes.heading: What Companies House does
scenes.narration: Companies House incorporates companies, receives annual accounts and the yearly confirmation statement, and keeps the public register of People with Significant Control, meaning anyone owning over 25 percent or with significant influence.

items.label: Incorporation
items.detail: Companies, LLPs, LPs, CICs and overseas companies

items.label: Statutory accounts
items.detail: Full, abridged, micro-entity or filleted; made public

items.label: Confirmation statement
items.detail: £34 digital, £62 paper from 1 May 2024

items.label: PSC register
items.detail: Shares, votes or significant influence

scenes.heading: Changes, capital, charges, strike-off
scenes.narration: Officer changes use AP01, TM01 and CH01 within 14 days. Shares use SH01, SH06 and SH19. Charges go on MR01 within 21 days or are void against a liquidator. Strike-off is voluntary via DS01 or compulsory.

items.label: Officers: AP01, TM01, CH01
items.detail: Appoint, terminate or change director details

items.label: Shares: SH01, SH06, SH19
items.detail: Allotment, cancellation, statement of capital

items.label: Charges: MR01
items.detail: Late charge is void against a liquidator

items.label: Strike-off: DS01
items.detail: Voluntary if solvent dormant; compulsory if overdue

scenes.heading: ECCTA 2023 reforms
scenes.narration: The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 is turning Companies House into more of a gatekeeper, in stages from 2024 to 2027. Always check the latest transition timetable before advising clients on first-year filings.

items.label: Identity verification
items.detail: Directors, PSCs and people filing for companies

items.label: Abridged accounts removed
items.detail: Filleted only; full accounts must still be prepared

items.label: Software-only filing
items.detail: Paper and WebFiling to be phased out

items.label: Stronger CH powers
items.detail: Query, reject and remove incorrect information

scenes.heading: Statutory filing deadlines
scenes.narration: Private company first accounts are due 21 months after incorporation, then 9 months after the accounting reference date. Public companies get 6 months. Officer changes take 14 days, charges 21 days.

items.label: Officer changes
items.detail: From change; criminal offence if missed

items.label: Charge registration MR01
items.detail: Late: void against liquidator, court needed

items.label: Public company accounts
items.detail: After accounting reference date

items.label: Private subsequent accounts
items.detail: After accounting reference date

items.label: Private first accounts
items.detail: After date of incorporation

scenes.heading: Penalties for late filing
scenes.narration: Late private company accounts cost £150 up to £1,500, public companies £750 up to £7,500, doubled if late twice running. A missed confirmation statement has no fine, but risks strike-off and prosecution of directors.

items.label: Private company accounts
items.detail: Up to 1 month late, to over 6 months; doubled if repeated

items.label: Public company accounts
items.detail: Doubled if late twice

items.label: Confirmation statement
items.detail: Due within 14 days; strike-off and prosecution risk

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Remember: Companies House is a registry gaining new powers under ECCTA, and its deadlines and penalties are strict. Know the forms and time limits so your clients stay compliant.

scenes.heading: The FRC and its successor ARGA
scenes.subheading: Who owns the UK standards you will apply when preparing accounts
scenes.narration: In this section we meet the Financial Reporting Council, known as the FRC, and the body replacing it. It matters because it owns the reporting standards you must apply when preparing accounts.

scenes.heading: What the FRC sets
scenes.narration: The FRC sets four big things: UK accounting standards, audit standards, the corporate governance code and the actuarial standards.

items.label: Accounting standards
items.detail: UK financial reporting standards

items.label: Audit standards
items.detail: International Standards on Auditing, UK version

items.label: Corporate governance code
items.detail: How companies should be run and overseen

items.label: Actuarial standards
items.detail: Standards for actuarial work

scenes.heading: From FRC to ARGA
scenes.narration: After the Kingman Review that followed Carillion's collapse, the FRC is being replaced by the Audit, Reporting and Governance Authority, or ARGA, which will have stronger statutory powers.

items.label: FRC
items.detail: Being replaced after the post-Carillion Kingman Review

items.label: ARGA
items.detail: Can directly sanction directors for reporting failures

scenes.heading: The core FRS standards
scenes.narration: FRS 100 tells you which standard applies to which entity. FRS 101 gives subsidiaries of IFRS groups reduced disclosure, and FRS 102 is the main UK GAAP standard most of your clients will use.

items.label: FRS 100
items.detail: Which standard applies to which entity

items.label: FRS 101
items.detail: Reduced disclosure for subsidiaries of IFRS groups

items.label: FRS 102
items.detail: The main UK GAAP standard, for most clients

items.label: FRS 102 Section 1A
items.detail: Reduced disclosures for Companies Act small entities

scenes.heading: Specialist and micro standards
scenes.narration: FRS 103 covers specialist insurance contracts and FRS 104 interim reporting. FRS 105 is the micro-entities regime: the simplest, with the fewest disclosures and no fair value model.

items.label: Insurance contracts
items.detail: Specialist standard

items.label: Interim reporting
items.detail: Interim financial reporting

items.label: Micro-entities regime
items.detail: Simplest, fewest disclosures, no fair value model

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Remember these points. We will study FRS 105, FRS 102 Section 1A and FRS 102 in granular detail in modules 29 to 32, including why each disclosure is required.

scenes.heading: Professional bodies and AML supervisors
scenes.subheading: Who awards accountancy designations, and who supervises members for AML
scenes.narration: To call yourself a Chartered Accountant, you must belong to a chartered body. These bodies set entry standards, run the qualification, monitor CPD and supervise members for anti-money laundering purposes.

scenes.heading: Chartered and audit-recognised bodies
scenes.narration: ICAEW is a full audit-recognised body, and you need a practising certificate for public practice. ICAS has the same scope in Scotland, Chartered Accountants Ireland works cross-border, and ACCA is the largest UK body.

items.label: ICAEW
items.detail: England & Wales; practising certificate for public practice

items.label: ICAS
items.detail: Same scope as ICAEW, within Scotland

items.label: Chartered Accts Ireland
items.detail: Cross-border: Northern Ireland and Republic of Ireland

items.label: ACCA
items.detail: Audit-recognised; largest UK body by membership

scenes.heading: Specialist bodies
scenes.narration: Some bodies specialise. CIMA focuses on management accounting and is not audit-recognised in the UK, while CIOT and ATT are a tax-only specialism.

items.label: CIMA
items.detail: Management accounting; also CGMA; not UK audit-recognised

items.label: CIOT / ATT
items.detail: Chartered Institute of Taxation and tax technicians

scenes.heading: Bookkeeping bodies and AML supervisors
scenes.narration: For bookkeeping and small-business work, AAT, ICB and IAB are all recognised anti-money laundering supervisors, so their members can be supervised without joining a chartered body.

items.label: AAT
items.detail: Ideal for bookkeeping and small-business accounting

items.label: ICB
items.detail: Institute of Certified Bookkeepers; AML supervisor

items.label: IAB
items.detail: Association of Bookkeepers; AML supervisor

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: Chartered Accountant requires chartered body membership, only some bodies are audit-recognised, and several bodies, including bookkeeping ones, act as anti-money laundering supervisors.

scenes.heading: OPBAS: Supervising the Supervisors
scenes.subheading: The Office for Professional Body AML Supervision and its role
scenes.narration: In this short section we meet the Office for Professional Body Anti-Money Laundering Supervision, known as OPBAS. It helps explain who keeps an eye on the bodies that supervise you.

scenes.heading: Where OPBAS Fits
scenes.narration: OPBAS sits within the Financial Conduct Authority and supervises the anti-money laundering supervisors. It does not supervise accountants directly; it makes sure the professional bodies do their supervisory job consistently.

items.label: Sits within the FCA
items.detail: Part of the Financial Conduct Authority

items.label: Supervises AML supervisors
items.detail: Oversees the professional bodies

items.label: Not accountants directly
items.detail: Accountants are supervised by their bodies

items.label: Ensures consistency
items.detail: Bodies must do their AML job consistently

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: OPBAS sits within the Financial Conduct Authority, oversees the professional bodies rather than you directly, and checks they supervise anti-money laundering consistently.

scenes.heading: AML supervision: you must be supervised
scenes.subheading: Why every accountancy or tax business needs an anti-money laundering supervisor
scenes.narration: In this section we look at anti-money laundering supervision, often called AML. If you provide accountancy or tax services as a business, being supervised is not optional, it is the law.

scenes.heading: Who supervises you?
scenes.narration: Under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017, as amended, anyone providing accountancy or tax services by way of business must be supervised, either by their professional body or, if not in one, directly by HMRC.

items.label: Your professional body
items.detail: If you are AAT, ACCA, ICAEW and so on

items.label: HMRC directly
items.detail: If you are not a member of a professional body

scenes.heading: Operating without supervision
scenes.narration: Trading without AML supervision is a criminal offence under regulation 56 of the 2017 Regulations, and it can carry up to two years in prison.

items.label: Criminal offence
items.detail: Up to two years' imprisonment, MLR 2017 regulation 56

scenes.heading: HMRC AML registration costs
scenes.narration: If HMRC supervises you, for 2024 to 2025 expect around £300 per premises each year, plus a £40 registration fee and a £150 fit and proper test for senior staff.

items.label: Annual fee per premises
items.detail: Approximate, 2024/25

items.label: Registration fee
items.detail: Paid on registering

items.label: Fit-and-proper test
items.detail: For senior staff

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: you must be supervised, your body or HMRC will do it, but never both, and going unsupervised is a crime. We cover AML in depth in Module 83.

scenes.heading: The ICO and data protection
scenes.subheading: Why accountants must register and protect the personal data they handle
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the Information Commissioner's Office, the ICO, which oversees data protection. As an accountant you handle lots of personal data, so this applies to you.

scenes.heading: Personal data accountants process
scenes.narration: Think about what crosses your desk every day: names, National Insurance numbers, salaries, bank details and addresses. All of that is personal data.

items.label: Names and addresses
items.detail: Basic identifying details of clients and staff

items.label: National Insurance numbers
items.detail: Often shortened to NINOs

items.label: Salaries
items.detail: Pay information for payroll and tax work

items.label: Bank details
items.detail: Account information for payments

scenes.heading: Registering with the ICO
scenes.narration: If your business processes personal data, you must register with the ICO and pay a notification fee, currently between forty pounds and two thousand nine hundred pounds a year depending on size.

items.label: Annual fee, lower end
items.detail: Notification fee for smaller businesses

items.label: Annual fee, upper end
items.detail: Fee rises depending on business size

scenes.heading: What you must do
scenes.narration: Registration is only half of it. You must also comply with the UK General Data Protection Regulation and the Data Protection Act 2018, which Module 86 covers in detail.

items.label: Register with the ICO
items.detail: Pay the annual notification fee

items.label: Comply with UK GDPR
items.detail: UK General Data Protection Regulation

items.label: Comply with DPA 2018
items.detail: Data Protection Act 2018; see Module 86

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: accountants process personal data, must register with the ICO and pay its fee, and must follow UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.

scenes.heading: The Pensions Regulator
scenes.subheading: Who enforces auto-enrolment, and why every employer must comply
scenes.narration: In this section we meet The Pensions Regulator, known as TPR. It enforces auto-enrolment compliance, which touches every employer you will ever work with.

scenes.heading: What every employer must do
scenes.narration: Every employer, regardless of size, has three duties: auto-enrol eligible jobholders into a qualifying pension scheme, pay at least the statutory minimum, and file an annual re-declaration of compliance.

items.label: Auto-enrol jobholders
items.detail: Eligible jobholders go into a qualifying pension scheme

items.label: Contribute the minimum
items.detail: Employer pays at least the statutory minimum

items.label: Re-declare compliance
items.detail: File a re-declaration of compliance every year

scenes.heading: Penalties for non-compliance
scenes.narration: Getting it wrong is costly. Penalties start with a fixed £400 and can escalate to £10,000 a day for the largest employers. We cover this in detail in Module 23.

items.label: Fixed penalty
items.detail: The starting point for non-compliance

items.label: Escalating penalty
items.detail: For the largest employers; see Module 23

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: TPR enforces auto-enrolment, every employer of any size has these duties, and penalties run from £400 up to £10,000 a day.

scenes.heading: The Charity Commission and OSCR
scenes.subheading: Who regulates charities across the UK, and how their accounts are prepared
scenes.narration: Charities have their own regulators and their own accounting rules. In this section we'll see who regulates charities in each part of the UK, and what framework their accounts follow.

scenes.heading: A regulator for each jurisdiction
scenes.narration: England and Wales use the Charity Commission for England and Wales. Scotland uses the Office of the Scottish Charity Regulator, known as OSCR, and Northern Ireland has its own Charity Commission.

items.label: England and Wales
items.detail: Charity Commission for England and Wales

items.label: Scotland
items.detail: Office of the Scottish Charity Regulator

items.label: Northern Ireland
items.detail: Charity Commission for Northern Ireland

scenes.heading: When to register in England and Wales
scenes.narration: A charity in England and Wales registers with the Charity Commission once its income exceeds five thousand pounds. A charitable incorporated organisation must register whatever its income.

items.label: Income threshold
items.detail: Register once income exceeds this amount

items.label: Charitable incorporated org
items.detail: CIOs register regardless of income

scenes.heading: How charity accounts are prepared
scenes.narration: Charity accounts follow the Charities SORP, the Statement of Recommended Practice based on FRS 102. It requires extensive narrative disclosure in the Trustees' Annual Report.

items.label: Charities SORP
items.detail: Statement of Recommended Practice

items.label: Based on FRS 102
items.detail: The underlying UK accounting standard

items.label: Trustees' Annual Report
items.detail: Extensive narrative disclosures

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember the three regulators, the five thousand pound threshold, and the Charities SORP. Module 71 covers charity conversion in depth.

scenes.heading: The Insolvency Service
scenes.subheading: Who handles business failure, bankruptcy and director disqualification
scenes.narration: Let's meet the Insolvency Service, the body that steps in when individuals or businesses fail. Knowing its role matters because you'll deal with it whenever a client's business ceases.

scenes.heading: What the Insolvency Service does
scenes.narration: It's part of the Department for Business and Trade. It investigates bankruptcies, supervises liquidators, oversees director disqualifications, and runs the Bankruptcy Restrictions and Director Disqualification regimes.

items.label: Investigates bankruptcies
items.detail: Looks into individual bankruptcies

items.label: Supervises liquidators
items.detail: Oversees those winding up companies

items.label: Director disqualification
items.detail: Oversees and runs this regime

items.label: Bankruptcy Restrictions
items.detail: Runs the Bankruptcy Restrictions regime

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: the Insolvency Service sits within the Department for Business and Trade, polices insolvency, and we'll see it again in modules 60 to 64 on cessation routes.

scenes.heading: A typical client's regulator map
scenes.subheading: One small company, eleven compliance points, several regulators
scenes.narration: Let's put the whole module together. Imagine you take on a brand-new private limited company, a husband-and-wife consultancy, and map every filing it owes and who receives it.

scenes.heading: HMRC filings
scenes.narration: HMRC receives the most: VAT returns quarterly if registered, a Full Payment Submission on or before each pay date, Self Assessment for each director by 31 January, P11Ds by 6 July if there are benefits, and the CT600.

items.label: RTI Full Payment Submission

items.label: Self Assessment

items.label: P11D and CT600
items.detail: P11D by 6 Jul if benefits; CT600 12 months after period end

scenes.heading: Other filings and frequencies
scenes.narration: Beyond HMRC: P60s go from employer to each employee by 31 May, Companies House gets the confirmation statement and statutory accounts yearly, and The Pensions Regulator wants a re-declaration every three years.

items.label: P60 to each employee

items.label: Confirmation statement

items.detail: The Pensions Regulator

scenes.narration: Add the annual ICO notification and your own anti-money laundering supervision, and that's eleven points for one tiny consultancy. Across thirty clients, workflow software like Karbon, Senta or Pixie becomes essential.

scenes.narration: To sum up the module: know who each regulator is, where their power comes from, and that even a small company client triggers around a dozen compliance points across at least four regulators.

scenes.heading: Seven UK business structures
scenes.subheading: Legal status, liability, tax, accounts and regulators at a glance
scenes.narration: In this section we compare the seven UK business structures side by side, because the structure decides who is liable, how profits are taxed, and who you report to.

scenes.heading: Unincorporated: no limited liability
scenes.narration: Sole traders and general partners face unlimited liability and pay income tax plus Class 2 and 4 National Insurance. Neither files public accounts, and only HMRC is involved.

items.label: Sole Trader
items.detail: Not separate; income tax plus Class 2 & 4 NI; HMRC only

items.label: General Partnership
items.detail: Not separate in England, separate in Scotland; tax per share

scenes.heading: LLP, Ltd and PLC
scenes.narration: These are separate legal entities filing public accounts with HMRC and Companies House. An LLP is tax transparent, while companies pay Corporation Tax, and a listed PLC also answers to the Financial Conduct Authority.

items.label: LLP
items.detail: Liability limited to capital; members pay IT and NI on share

items.label: Limited (Ltd)
items.detail: Limited to share capital; shareholders pay IT or dividend tax

items.label: PLC
items.detail: Extensive public accounts; FCA too if listed

scenes.heading: Social and charitable structures
scenes.narration: A Community Interest Company pays Corporation Tax and files a CIC34 report for the CIC Regulator. Charities and CIOs are generally exempt, often using a trading subsidiary, and follow the Charities SORP.

items.label: CIC
items.detail: Ltd or by guarantee; accounts plus CIC34 report

items.label: Charity / CIO
items.detail: Generally exempt; trading subsidiary often used

items.label: Charity regulators
items.detail: Charity Commission, OSCR or CCNI, plus CH if a company

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: liability, tax treatment, public accounts and regulators all follow from the structure you choose. Learn this table well, it underpins the rest of the module.

scenes.heading: Sole trader: the legal nuts and bolts
scenes.subheading: No legal separation between person and business, and what that means for tax
scenes.narration: A sole trader trades in their own name, with no legal separation from the business. Their assets are the business assets in law, so if the business goes bankrupt, personal assets follow.

scenes.heading: Registering as a sole trader
scenes.narration: Register for Self Assessment with HMRC online by 5 October after the end of the tax year you started. HMRC then issues a Unique Taxpayer Reference within about ten working days, plus a separate Government Gateway login.

items.label: Register online
items.detail: After the end of the tax year you started trading

items.label: UTR issued
items.detail: Unique Taxpayer Reference, about 10 working days

items.label: Gateway login
items.detail: Separate Government Gateway login also issued

scenes.heading: Tax on profits: 2024/25
scenes.narration: Income Tax applies above the twelve thousand, five hundred and seventy pound Personal Allowance at 20, 40 and 45 percent. The allowance tapers by one pound for every two above one hundred thousand, gone at one hundred and twenty-five thousand, one hundred and forty.

items.label: Personal Allowance
items.detail: 2024/25, tapers £1 per £2 above £100,000

items.label: Income Tax rates
items.detail: Basic, higher and additional rates

items.label: Allowance fully lost
items.detail: Personal Allowance fully eroded at this income

scenes.heading: National Insurance for sole traders
scenes.narration: Class 4 National Insurance is 6 percent on profits between twelve thousand, five hundred and seventy and fifty thousand, two hundred and seventy pounds, then 2 percent. Flat-rate Class 2 was abolished from 6 April 2024, but voluntary contributions remain.

items.label: Class 4 main rate
items.detail: Profits £12,570 to £50,270; cut from 9% from 6 April 2024

items.label: Class 4 upper rate
items.detail: Profits above £50,270

items.label: Class 2 flat rate
items.detail: Weekly charge abolished from 6 April 2024

items.label: Voluntary Class 2
items.detail: Profits under £6,725, to keep a state pension year

scenes.heading: Sarah, freelance graphic designer
scenes.narration: Sarah's forty thousand pound profit gives taxable income of twenty-seven thousand, four hundred and thirty. She pays seven thousand, one hundred and thirty-two pounds in total, due by 31 January 2026.

items.label: Trading profit
items.detail: Year ended 5 April 2025, no other income

items.label: Income Tax at 20%
items.detail: On taxable income of £27,430
