scenes.heading: Pros and cons of sole trader status
scenes.narration: It's cheap, simple and private, with sideways loss relief and the cash basis under one hundred and fifty thousand turnover. But liability is unlimited, equity finance is out, and profits are taxed yearly regardless of drawings.

items.label: Advantages
items.detail: No fees, private, loss relief, cash basis, one SA100

items.label: Disadvantages
items.detail: Unlimited liability, no equity, ~28% basic marginal rate

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: no legal separation, register by 5 October, Income Tax plus Class 4 on profits, and weigh simplicity against unlimited liability.

scenes.heading: General Partnership
scenes.subheading: Two or more persons in business together with a view to profit
scenes.narration: Let's look at the general partnership: two or more persons, individuals or companies, carrying on business in common with a view to profit, as defined in section 1 of the Partnership Act 1890.

scenes.heading: No separate legal person
scenes.narration: In England and Wales a partnership has no legal personality of its own, so each partner is jointly and severally liable for all the partnership's debts.

items.label: No legal personality
items.detail: In England & Wales the firm is not a separate person

items.label: Joint and several liability
items.detail: Each partner is liable for partnership debts

scenes.heading: Default rules vs agreement
scenes.narration: The 1890 Act sets default rules, like equal profit sharing and no pay for working in the business. Almost all clients override these with a written Partnership Agreement.

items.label: Partnership Act 1890
items.detail: Equal profits, equal capital, no remuneration

items.label: Partnership Agreement
items.detail: Written terms that override the defaults

scenes.heading: What the agreement covers
scenes.narration: A good agreement covers the profit-sharing ratio, capital and interest on it, partner salaries, drawings, partners joining or leaving, disputes, and what happens on a partner's death. Salaries are a profit and loss charge but added back for tax.

items.label: Profit-sharing ratio
items.detail: The ratio and any changes to it

items.label: Capital and salaries
items.detail: Interest on capital; salaries added back for tax

items.label: Drawings and partners
items.detail: Drawings limits; admission and retirement

items.label: Disputes and death
items.detail: Dispute resolution; continuation or dissolution

scenes.heading: How a partnership is taxed
scenes.narration: The partnership itself pays no tax. It reports its profit on the SA800, the profit is split by profit-sharing ratio, and each partner reports their share on the SA104 pages within their personal SA100.

items.label: File SA800
items.detail: Partnership Tax Return reports the firm's profit

items.label: Allocate by PSR
items.detail: Profit split using the period's profit-sharing ratio

items.label: Partners file SA104
items.detail: Partnership pages within each personal SA100

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Finally, remember the limited partnership: at least one general partner with unlimited liability, limited partners liable up to their capital, registered at Companies House under the 1907 Act, mostly for private equity funds. It is not an LLP.

scenes.heading: Limited Liability Partnerships
scenes.subheading: A separate legal entity like a company, but taxed like a partnership
scenes.narration: Welcome to limited liability partnerships, created by the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000. They were designed for professional firms like law and accountancy practices wanting limited liability without becoming companies.

scenes.heading: Company-like law, partnership tax
scenes.narration: Legally, an LLP is a separate entity, just like a company. For tax, though, it is transparent like a partnership, so members pay income tax and National Insurance on their share.

items.label: Legal status
items.detail: Separate legal entity, like a company

items.label: Tax treatment
items.detail: Transparent: members pay income tax and NI on their share

scenes.heading: Key LLP attributes
scenes.narration: An LLP needs at least two members, and at least two designated members who carry the statutory filing duties. There is no share capital; capital contributions are treated as members' loans or equity under the LLP agreement.

items.label: Members
items.detail: An LLP needs at least two members

items.label: Designated members
items.detail: They carry the statutory filing duties

items.label: No share capital
items.detail: Contributions are members' loans or equity per agreement

scenes.heading: Annual filing at Companies House
scenes.narration: Every year, an LLP files annual accounts at Companies House, with small and micro exemptions broadly mirroring companies. It also files a confirmation statement annually.

items.label: Annual accounts
items.detail: Small and micro exemptions broadly mirror companies

items.label: Confirmation statement
items.detail: Filed at Companies House every year

scenes.heading: Taxing members and salaried members
scenes.narration: Members are taxed personally on their profit share as if partners, under ITTOIA 2005 section 863. But the salaried members rule treats some disguised employees as employees for PAYE and National Insurance, so apply the three-condition test every year.

items.label: Profit share taxed
items.detail: ITTOIA 2005: members taxed as if they were partners

items.label: Salaried members rule
items.detail: ITA 2007: disguised employees treated as employees

items.label: Three-condition test
items.detail: Must be applied every year for PAYE and NI

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: separate legal entity, partnership-style tax, at least two members and two designated members, no share capital, annual filings, and test salaried members every year.

scenes.heading: Private Limited Company (Ltd)
scenes.subheading: The workhorse of UK business, with around 4.6 million companies registered
scenes.narration: The private limited company is the workhorse of UK business, with roughly 4.6 million on the register. It is a separate legal person: shareholders own it and directors manage it.

scenes.heading: Constitutional documents
scenes.narration: Three documents shape a company. The Articles are public and filed at Companies House, but a Shareholders' Agreement is a private contract, so it is not filed.

items.label: Memorandum of Association
items.detail: Short; subscribers confirm intent to form company

items.label: Articles of Association
items.detail: Internal rulebook; Model Articles are the default

items.label: Shareholders' Agreement
items.detail: Private contract: pre-emption, exit, valuation

scenes.heading: Two layers of tax
scenes.narration: A company pays Corporation Tax on its profits, then the owner pays Income Tax on what they take out, whether as salary under Pay As You Earn or as dividends.

items.label: Corporation Tax main rate
items.detail: Profits above £250,000

items.label: Small profits rate
items.detail: Profits up to £50,000; marginal relief between

items.label: Basic rate dividend tax
items.detail: Higher 33.75%, additional 39.35%

items.label: Dividend allowance 2024/25
items.detail: Down from £1,000 in 2023/24

scenes.heading: Salary and dividend mix
scenes.narration: The classic plan is a salary at the Secondary Threshold to keep a State Pension qualifying year without National Insurance, then dividends. From April 2025 that plan needs revisiting.

items.label: 2024/25 classic plan
items.detail: Salary at Secondary Threshold, rest as dividends

items.label: From 6 April 2025
items.detail: Employer NI 15%; salary up to £12,570 may suit

scenes.heading: Director with £40,000 profit
scenes.narration: On £40,000 profit, the director pays £7,714 in total, about 19.3 percent. That is slightly more than a sole trader's £7,132, so the company's value shows at higher profits and with limited liability.

items.label: Salary taken
items.detail: Covered by the Personal Allowance

items.label: Corporation Tax at 19%
items.detail: On £30,900 profit after salary

items.label: Dividend tax at 8.75%
items.detail: On £21,059 taxable dividend

items.label: Total tax
items.detail: Sole trader pays £7,132 on the same profit

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: separate legal person, public Articles but private agreements, two layers of tax, and a salary and dividend mix to review from April 2025.

scenes.heading: Public Limited Company (PLC)
scenes.subheading: What the "plc" label means and the extra rules that come with it
scenes.narration: A public limited company is one whose name ends in plc. The label means it can offer shares to the public, but not that it must, and not that it is listed on a stock exchange.

scenes.heading: Share capital requirements
scenes.narration: A PLC needs minimum allotted share capital of fifty thousand pounds, and at least twenty-five percent of that must be paid up.

items.label: Minimum allotted capital
items.detail: Required for every PLC

items.label: Must be paid up
items.detail: Of the minimum allotted share capital

scenes.heading: PLC versus Ltd: officers
scenes.narration: A PLC must have at least two directors, compared with one for a private limited company, and appointing a company secretary is mandatory.

items.label: PLC
items.detail: Minimum 2 directors plus a mandatory company secretary

items.label: Ltd
items.detail: Minimum of 1 director

scenes.heading: Accounts filing deadlines
scenes.narration: PLCs have less time to file. Accounts are due six months after the accounting reference date, compared with nine months for a private limited company.

items.label: PLC accounts due
items.detail: After the accounting reference date

items.label: Ltd accounts due
items.detail: After the accounting reference date

scenes.heading: Reporting and listing rules
scenes.narration: A PLC cannot file abridged or filleted accounts, so full accounts are always required. If it is listed, Financial Conduct Authority rules apply on top.

items.label: Full accounts only
items.detail: No abridged or filleted accounts allowed

items.label: If listed
items.detail: LSE Main, AIM or AQUIS: FCA rules apply on top

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: plc means it can offer shares publicly, it needs fifty thousand pounds of capital, two directors and a secretary, and it files full accounts within six months.

scenes.heading: Community Interest Companies
scenes.subheading: A limited company with a locked-in community and social purpose
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the Community Interest Company, often called a CIC. It matters because it blends a normal limited company with a legal promise to benefit the community.

scenes.heading: What a CIC is
scenes.narration: A CIC is a limited company, either limited by shares or by guarantee, with a community purpose lock. It was created by the Companies Audit, Investigations and Community Enterprise Act 2004.

items.label: Company limited by shares
items.detail: Can be set up as a standard Ltd company

items.label: Limited by guarantee
items.detail: Or as a company limited by guarantee

items.label: Created by statute
items.detail: Companies (Audit, Investigations & Community Enterprise) Act

scenes.heading: Regulation and annual reporting
scenes.narration: CICs are regulated by the CIC Regulator, a small office within Companies House. Each year the CIC files a CIC34 community interest report alongside its accounts.

items.label: Regulated by CIC Regulator
items.detail: A small office within Companies House

items.label: Prepare annual accounts
items.detail: Filed each year as for a limited company

items.label: File CIC34 report
items.detail: Community interest report filed with the accounts

scenes.heading: The asset lock
scenes.narration: The asset lock is the key feature: assets cannot be distributed to members. If the CIC is dissolved, its assets must transfer to another asset-locked body, so they stay working for the community.

items.label: No distribution to members
items.detail: Assets cannot be paid out to members

items.label: On dissolution
items.detail: Assets must go to another asset-locked body

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: a CIC is a limited company with a community lock, created in 2004, regulated by the CIC Regulator, filing a CIC34 yearly, and bound by an asset lock.

scenes.heading: Charities, CIOs and Charitable Companies
scenes.subheading: The three main legal forms a charity can take, and how they are taxed
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the three principal forms a charity can take. Choosing the right one matters, because it decides who is personally liable and which regulators the charity answers to.

scenes.heading: Three principal forms
scenes.narration: An unincorporated charity has no separate legal personality, so its trustees are personally liable. A charitable company has its own legal personality, and so does a Charitable Incorporated Organisation, or CIO.

items.label: Unincorporated charity
items.detail: Trust or association; trustees personally liable

items.label: Charitable company
items.detail: Limited by guarantee; separate legal personality

items.label: CIO
items.detail: Charitable Incorporated Organisation

scenes.heading: Company versus CIO: regulators
scenes.narration: A charitable company is dual-registered with Companies House and the Charity Commission. A CIO, created by Part 11 of the Charities Act 2011, has a single regulator, so there's no Companies House filing burden.

items.label: Charitable company
items.detail: Companies House plus Charity Commission

items.label: CIO
items.detail: Charity Commission only; no Companies House filing

scenes.heading: Two flavours of CIO
scenes.narration: CIOs come in two flavours. In a Foundation CIO the members are the trustees, while an Association CIO has a separate membership body that elects the trustees.

items.label: Foundation CIO
items.detail: The members are the trustees

items.label: Association CIO
items.detail: Separate members elect the trustees

scenes.heading: How charities are taxed
scenes.narration: Most charity income is exempt under Part 11 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010, provided it's used for charitable purposes. Trading outside the primary purpose is sometimes run through a wholly-owned subsidiary that gift-aids its profit to the parent.

items.label: Income exempt
items.detail: CTA 2010 Part 11, if used for charitable purposes

items.label: Non-primary trading
items.detail: Routed through a wholly-owned trading subsidiary

items.label: Gift Aid to parent
items.detail: Subsidiary gift-aids its profit up to the charity

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember the three forms, who regulates each, the two CIO flavours and the tax exemption. Converting a limited company into a CIO is covered in detail in Module 71.

scenes.heading: The choice tree: which structure?
scenes.subheading: Matching each client situation to the right business structure
scenes.narration: In this section we match real client situations to the right business structure. Getting this right protects your client and saves them tax and admin, so it is a core advisory skill.

scenes.heading: Sole trader or Ltd?
scenes.narration: Hobby income under ten thousand pounds and freelancers on twenty to forty thousand usually suit sole trader. Tradespeople on thirty thousand plus, and two-person consultancies retaining profit, usually suit a limited company.

items.label: Hobby, under £10k profit
items.detail: Simplest, cheapest; no CT or Companies House filings

items.label: Freelancer £20k to £40k
items.detail: Similar tax, cheaper admin; revisit at £50k+

items.label: Tradesperson £30k+
items.detail: Protection from injury or property-damage liability

items.label: Two-person consultancy
items.detail: Income splitting via dividends; defer retained profit

scenes.heading: Property landlords
scenes.narration: A single rental property generally stays in personal name, but needs modelling. A portfolio of five or more usually suits a limited company, because Section 24 makes personal interest costly while companies fully deduct it.

items.label: Single rental property
items.detail: 3% SDLT surcharge and extra 8% CGT if corporate; model it

items.label: Portfolio of 5+ properties
items.detail: Section 24 costly personally; companies deduct interest

scenes.heading: Specialist structures
scenes.narration: Professional firms suit an LLP. Social enterprises use a CIC if mostly trading or a CIO if mostly grant-funded. Charities suit a CIO, and venture capital backed businesses need Ltd or PLC shares.

items.label: Professional firm
items.detail: Limited liability, tax transparency, easy member changes

items.label: Social enterprise
items.detail: Asset lock; CIO if grant-funded, CIC if trading

items.label: Charity raising funds
items.detail: Single regulator, trustee limited liability

items.label: SME with VC funding
items.detail: Shares suit equity investors; partnerships don't

scenes.heading: The £50k profit pivot
scenes.narration: As a rule of thumb, sole trader is usually cheaper up to thirty thousand, it is broadly equal to fifty thousand, and above that Ltd dominates, unless the owner extracts everything. Always model actual numbers.

items.label: Up to £30k profit
items.detail: Usually cheaper after software and accountancy costs

items.label: £30k to £50k profit
items.detail: Broadly equivalent

items.label: Above £50k profit
items.detail: Unless owner extracts every penny; dividend tax narrows it

scenes.heading: Module 2 key takeaways
scenes.narration: To sum up Module 2: seven structures, each trading off liability, tax and disclosure. Always model the after-tax outcome, as the 2024/25 to 2025/26 changes shift the balance.

scenes.heading: What is bookkeeping?
scenes.subheading: The systematic, chronological record of every financial transaction
scenes.narration: Welcome to bookkeeping, the foundation of everything you'll do as an accountant. Let's see what it is and why every business depends on it.

scenes.heading: Why businesses keep books
scenes.narration: Recording every transaction in date order lets a business know its position, measure its performance, prove its figures to outsiders, and spot errors and fraud.

items.label: Financial position
items.detail: Know where it stands at any moment: the balance sheet

items.label: Performance
items.detail: Measure results over a period: the profit and loss

items.label: Proof to outsiders
items.detail: HMRC, Companies House, banks and investors

items.label: Errors and fraud
items.detail: Detect mistakes and wrongdoing

scenes.heading: An old, unchanged discipline
scenes.narration: Bookkeeping is around 700 years old. The Italian friar Luca Pacioli codified it in Summa de Arithmetica in 1494, and the underlying logic hasn't changed since.

items.label: Codified by Luca Pacioli
items.detail: Set out in Summa de Arithmetica

items.label: Same logic today
items.detail: About 700 years old, logic unchanged

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: bookkeeping records every transaction systematically and in order, serves four purposes, and rests on logic that has lasted centuries.

scenes.heading: The accounting equation
scenes.subheading: Assets = Liabilities + Equity, true after every single transaction
scenes.narration: Welcome to the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity. It's the only equation in accounting, and it holds after every transaction, in every business, in every era.

scenes.heading: Three ways to write it
scenes.narration: The core equation has useful variations. Rearranged, assets minus liabilities gives equity, or net worth, and that's how the balance sheet is normally presented in the UK.

items.label: Core equation
items.detail: Assets = Liabilities + Equity

items.label: UK balance sheet view
items.detail: Assets − Liabilities = Equity, or net worth

scenes.heading: Expanding equity over time
scenes.narration: Equity builds up over time: start with the capital introduced, add retained profits, then take away drawings or dividends paid out to the owners.

items.label: Capital introduced
items.detail: What the owners put into the business

items.label: Add retained profits
items.detail: Profits kept in the business

items.label: Less drawings or dividends
items.detail: Amounts taken out by the owners

scenes.heading: Profit and the change in equity
scenes.narration: Profit equals income minus expenses. It measures the change in equity from operations between two balance sheet dates, leaving out capital put in or taken out.

items.label: Profit
items.detail: Income − Expenses: change in equity from operations

items.label: Excluded from profit
items.detail: Capital introduced or withdrawn by the owners

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: one equation, always in balance, with a few handy rearrangements for the balance sheet, equity and profit.

scenes.heading: Double-entry: the symmetry rule
scenes.subheading: Every transaction has equal and opposite debits and credits
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the heart of double-entry. Every transaction is recorded on two sides, and knowing which side is which is the skill everything else rests on.

scenes.heading: Two equal and opposite entries
scenes.narration: Every transaction has at least one debit and one credit, or several entries that add up to balance. That symmetry is what guarantees the accounting equation always stays true.

items.label: Debit
items.detail: At least one debit entry per transaction

items.label: Credit
items.detail: Equal total of credits, so the equation holds

scenes.heading: Debit increases, debit balance
scenes.narration: Assets, expenses and drawings all increase with a debit and decrease with a credit. Their normal balance is a debit.

items.label: Asset
items.detail: Increase debit, decrease credit, normal balance debit

items.label: Expense
items.detail: Increase debit, decrease credit, normal balance debit

items.label: Drawings
items.detail: Increase debit, decrease credit, normal balance debit

scenes.heading: Credit increases, credit balance
scenes.narration: Liabilities, equity or capital, and income or revenue work the other way. They increase with a credit, decrease with a debit, and normally carry a credit balance.

items.label: Liability
items.detail: Increase credit, decrease debit, normal balance credit

items.label: Equity or Capital
items.detail: Increase credit, decrease debit, normal balance credit

items.label: Income or Revenue
items.detail: Increase credit, decrease debit, normal balance credit

scenes.heading: Remember it: DEAD CLIC
scenes.narration: Here's a handy memory aid, DEAD CLIC. Debits go up for expenses, assets and drawings; credits go up for liabilities, income and capital.

items.label: DEAD
items.detail: Debits up: Expenses, Assets, Drawings

items.label: CLIC
items.detail: Credits up: Liabilities, Income, Capital

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: debits always equal credits, the account type fixes the direction, and DEAD CLIC will keep you right every time.

scenes.heading: The 8 universal transaction patterns
scenes.subheading: Every UK business transaction reduces to one of eight double-entry patterns
scenes.narration: Every UK business transaction reduces to one of eight patterns. Memorise them, and you can journalise anything that comes across your desk.

scenes.heading: Patterns 1 and 2: making a sale
scenes.narration: A cash sale debits Bank and credits Sales together. A credit sale debits Trade Debtors, then credits Sales of 1,000 and VAT Output Tax of 200, recognising revenue at the point of supply.

items.label: 1. Cash sale
items.detail: Dr Bank, Cr Sales or Sales plus VAT control

items.label: 2. Credit sale
items.detail: Dr Trade Debtors; Cr Sales 1,000, VAT Output Tax 200

scenes.heading: Pattern 3: receipt from a customer
scenes.narration: When the credit customer pays, debit Bank and credit Trade Debtors with 1,200. The revenue was already recorded in pattern 2, so never record the sale again.

items.label: Don't record sales twice
items.detail: Dr Bank, Cr Trade Debtors; this only settles the receivable

scenes.heading: Patterns 4 to 6: buying and paying
scenes.narration: A cash purchase credits Bank straight away. A credit purchase credits Trade Creditors instead, and paying the supplier later debits Trade Creditors and credits Bank.

items.label: 4. Cash purchase
items.detail: Dr Stationery 50, VAT Input Tax 10 if recoverable; Cr Bank

items.label: 5. Credit purchase
items.detail: Dr Expense or Asset 100, VAT Input 20; Cr Trade Creditors

items.label: 6. Payment to supplier
items.detail: Dr Trade Creditors, Cr Bank

scenes.heading: Patterns 7 and 8: owner money
scenes.narration: When the owner puts money in, debit Bank and credit Capital, Director's Loan or Share Capital. When money goes out to the owner, debit Drawings or Dividends Paid and credit Bank.

items.label: 7. Capital introduced
items.detail: Dr Bank; Cr Capital, Director's Loan or Share Capital

items.label: 8. Drawings or dividend
items.detail: Dr Drawings or Dividends Paid; Cr Bank

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Learn these eight patterns by heart. Watch where VAT sits, and remember customer receipts and supplier payments only settle balances already recorded.

items.label: Output VAT Cr, input VAT Dr

scenes.heading: Compound journals
scenes.subheading: When one transaction needs more than two postings, such as payroll
scenes.narration: Some transactions need more than two postings, and payroll is the classic case. For these we use a compound journal, and it still has to balance.

scenes.heading: The monthly payroll figures
scenes.narration: Here is our month's payroll: gross pay of ten thousand pounds, tax of fifteen hundred, employee National Insurance of seven hundred, employer National Insurance of nine hundred, and net pay of seven thousand eight hundred.

items.label: Employee and employer NI
items.detail: Employee NI £700, employer NI £900

scenes.heading: Debits and credits
scenes.narration: We debit wages and salaries with ten thousand and employer's National Insurance with nine hundred, both in profit and loss. We credit the tax and National Insurance liability with three thousand one hundred, and net wages payable or bank with seven thousand eight hundred.

items.label: Debits
items.detail: Wages & Salaries £10,000; Employer's NI £900

items.label: Credits
items.detail: PAYE/NIC liability £3,100; Net wages payable £7,800

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: use a compound journal when you need more than two postings, and always check that total debits equal total credits.

items.label: Employer NI is a P&L cost

scenes.heading: The trial balance
scenes.subheading: What it proves, what it misses, and the other month-end checks
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the trial balance, a list of every ledger balance. It's a vital check, but knowing its limits is just as important for a trainee accountant.

scenes.heading: How a trial balance works
scenes.narration: You list every ledger account balance, debits in one column and credits in the other. If both columns total the same figure, you have arithmetic integrity.

items.label: List every balance
items.detail: Every ledger account balance goes on the list

items.label: Split into two columns
items.detail: Debits in one column, credits in the other

items.label: Compare the totals
items.detail: Equal totals prove arithmetic integrity

scenes.heading: What a trial balance can catch
scenes.narration: A trial balance spots errors that leave the sides unequal, like one-sided entries or casting errors. But six error types keep debits and credits equal, so they slip straight through.

items.label: Will detect
items.detail: One-sided entries, different Dr and Cr amounts, casting, transpositions

items.label: Will not detect
items.detail: Omission, commission, principle, compensating, original entry, reversal

scenes.heading: Errors that slip through
scenes.narration: For example, an error of principle is expensing capital spending as a repair, and a reversal error swaps the debit and credit. The columns still agree, so the trial balance stays silent.

items.label: Omission and commission
items.detail: Not recorded at all, or right side but wrong account

items.label: Principle
items.detail: e.g. capital expenditure expensed as a repair

items.label: Compensating
items.detail: Two errors that cancel each other out

items.label: Original entry and reversal
items.detail: Wrong amount on both sides, or Dr and Cr swapped

scenes.heading: The three month-end checks
scenes.narration: That's why the trial balance is necessary but not sufficient. Alongside it, the bank reconciliation proves cash against the bank statement, and control account reconciliations prove debtors and creditors against the sub-ledgers.

items.label: Trial balance
items.detail: Proves arithmetic integrity

items.label: Bank reconciliation
items.detail: Cash account against external bank statement

items.label: Control account recs
items.detail: Debtor and creditor controls against sub-ledgers

scenes.heading: Module 3 key takeaways
scenes.narration: To wrap up Module 3: the accounting equation always holds, every transaction has equal debits and credits, and the trial balance proves arithmetic but not everything.

items.label: Equal Dr and Cr: DEAD CLIC

scenes.heading: What is the chart of accounts?
scenes.subheading: The backbone of the accounting system
scenes.narration: Welcome to section 4.1. We're looking at the chart of accounts, the list that sits behind everything you post, so getting it right makes every report easier.

scenes.heading: The list of every ledger account
scenes.narration: The chart of accounts lists every account in the general ledger, organised by code or category. Everything that gets posted lands in one of these accounts.

items.label: Every account
items.detail: All general ledger accounts in one list

items.label: Organised by code
items.detail: Or grouped by category

items.label: Where postings land
items.detail: Every posting goes to one of these accounts

scenes.heading: What a good structure makes easy
scenes.narration: The structure decides how easily you can produce a profit and loss account, a balance sheet, a VAT return and statutory accounts mapped to the Companies Act formats.

items.label: Profit and loss
items.detail: Income and expense classification

items.label: Balance sheet
items.detail: Asset, liability and equity classification

items.label: VAT return
items.detail: Driven by VAT codes

items.label: Statutory accounts
items.detail: Mapped to the Companies Act formats

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: the chart of accounts lists every ledger account, every posting lands in one, and its structure shapes how easily you can report.

scenes.heading: Standard UK Chart of Accounts
scenes.subheading: How Xero and QBO default codes group accounts into categories
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the standard UK chart of accounts, using the Xero and QuickBooks Online defaults. Knowing the code ranges helps you find and post to the right account quickly.

scenes.heading: Income and expense code ranges
scenes.narration: Sales and revenue sit in 100 to 199, cost of sales in 300 to 399, operating expenses such as rent and salaries in 400 to 599, and finance or other items in 600 to 699.

items.label: Sales / Revenue
items.detail: 200 Sales, 260 Other Income

items.label: Cost of Sales
items.detail: 310 Materials, 320 Direct Labour

items.label: Operating Expenses
items.detail: 404 Rent, 408 Utilities, 412 Insurance, 477 Salaries

items.label: Finance / Other
items.detail: 610 Interest Income, 620 Bank Charges, 625 Loan Interest

scenes.heading: Depreciation, tax and assets
scenes.narration: Depreciation and tax charges use 700 to 799. Non-current assets like equipment and vehicles use 800 to 899, current assets 900 to 989, and prepayments and accrued income 990 to 999.

items.label: Depreciation, Tax Charges
items.detail: 710 Depreciation, 760 Corporation Tax

items.label: Non-current Assets
items.detail: 810 Office Equipment, 820 Plant, 850 Motor Vehicles

items.label: Current Assets
items.detail: 910 Inventory, 920 Trade Debtors, 950 Bank, 960 Petty Cash

items.label: Prepayments & Accrued Inc.
items.detail: 995 Prepayments, 996 Accrued Income

scenes.heading: Liabilities and equity
scenes.narration: Current liabilities, such as trade creditors, VAT and PAYE, use 1000 to 1099. Accruals and deferred income use 1100 to 1199, non-current liabilities 1200 to 1299, and equity 1500 to 1599.

items.label: Current Liabilities
items.detail: 1020 Trade Creditors, 1040 VAT, 1050 PAYE/NIC, 1060 CT

items.label: Accruals & Deferred Income
items.detail: 1110 Accruals, 1120 Deferred Income

items.label: Non-current Liabilities
items.detail: 1210 Bank Loans, 1230 Hire Purchase

items.label: Equity
items.detail: 1510 Share Capital, 1530 Retained Earnings, 1560 Dividends

scenes.heading: Watch out when converting platforms
scenes.narration: Xero, QuickBooks Online, Sage and FreeAgent each use slightly different default code numbers, though the categories are universal. So when moving a client, map the chart of accounts first, as it causes the most conversion errors.

items.label: Codes differ by platform
items.detail: Xero, QBO, Sage, FreeAgent vary; categories are universal

items.label: Map the COA first
items.detail: Most common source of conversion errors

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Let's recap the key points before we talk them through together.

scenes.heading: Control accounts and sub-ledgers
scenes.subheading: How single-line balances in the general ledger summarise the detail beneath
scenes.narration: In this section we look at control accounts, the single-line balances in the general ledger that summarise a sub-ledger. Getting them right keeps your books trustworthy and your reports clean.

scenes.heading: Four common control accounts
scenes.narration: Each control account is a summary, and the sub-ledger behind it holds the detail. For debtors that's every customer's balance, shown in the Aged Debtors Report, and for creditors it's every supplier's balance.

items.label: Trade Debtors Control
items.detail: Detail: each customer's balance, Aged Debtors Report

items.label: Trade Creditors Control
items.detail: Detail: supplier balances, Aged Creditors

items.label: VAT Control
items.detail: Detail: transaction-level VAT by tax code

items.label: PAYE/NIC Control
items.detail: Detail: month-by-month payroll

scenes.heading: Reconcile every period
scenes.narration: A control account must agree to its sub-ledger every period. If it doesn't, something was posted straight to the control account, often a manual journal that should have been a customer credit note.

items.label: Control and sub-ledger differ
items.detail: An entry has bypassed the sub-ledger

items.label: Common cause
items.detail: Manual journal used instead of a customer credit note

scenes.heading: Module 4 key takeaways
scenes.narration: To wrap up Module 4: the chart of accounts lists every ledger account by category, control accounts must always reconcile, and good design lets you produce a clean VAT return, CT600 and statutory accounts.

items.label: Design with end report in mind

scenes.heading: The Bookkeeping Cycle in 9 Steps
scenes.subheading: From source document to trial balance, management accounts and a locked period
scenes.narration: Every month, good bookkeeping follows the same nine steps, from gathering paperwork to locking the period. Let's walk through them in order, because each step builds on the one before.

scenes.heading: Steps 1 to 3: Capture, Post, Reconcile
scenes.narration: First, capture every source document, from tools like Dext, supplier portals and bank feeds. Then code and post each item, and match every bank statement line to a posting, investigating anything unmatched.

items.label: Capture source documents
items.detail: Invoices, receipts, bank statements, expenses, payroll

items.label: Code and post
items.detail: Assign a chart of accounts code and VAT code, then post

items.label: Reconcile the bank
items.detail: Match every statement line; investigate unmatched items

scenes.heading: Step 4: Reconcile Control Accounts
scenes.narration: Next, check each control account against its supporting report: debtors to the receivables ageing, creditors to the payables ageing, VAT to the draft return, and Pay As You Earn to the payroll summary.

items.label: Debtors control
items.detail: Agree to accounts receivable ageing

items.label: Creditors control
items.detail: Agree to accounts payable ageing

items.label: VAT control
items.detail: Agree to the VAT return draft

items.label: PAYE control
items.detail: Agree to the payroll summary

scenes.heading: Steps 5 to 7: Adjust, Test, Report
scenes.narration: Post adjusting journals such as accruals, prepayments and depreciation. Then run a trial balance to confirm debits equal credits and spot odd balances, before producing management accounts.

items.label: Adjusting journals
items.detail: Accruals, prepayments, depreciation, stock, deferred income

items.label: Run a trial balance
items.detail: Review unusual balances, like negative assets

items.label: Management accounts
items.detail: Profit and loss vs budget, balance sheet, key KPIs

scenes.heading: Steps 8 and 9: Lock and Archive
scenes.narration: Set a lock date in your software so nobody can post into a prior period. Finally, file the source documents, save the management pack and log the version.

items.label: Lock the period
items.detail: Lock date blocks prior-period postings

items.label: File and archive
items.detail: Store documents, save pack, log version

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: capture and post everything, reconcile the bank and control accounts, adjust, prove the trial balance, report, then lock and archive.

scenes.heading: Bank reconciliation in depth
scenes.subheading: Does your cash book agree with the bank's record of your cash?
scenes.narration: In this section we look closely at bank reconciliation. It answers one simple question: does your cash book agree with the bank's own record of your cash?

scenes.heading: How the reconciliation works
scenes.narration: You start from the bank statement closing balance, then adjust for unpresented cheques, uncleared lodgements and bank-only items, until you arrive at the cash book balance.

items.label: Start: bank closing balance
items.detail: The balance shown on the bank statement

items.label: Unpresented cheques
items.detail: Cheques written but not yet through the bank

items.label: Uncleared lodgements
items.detail: Money banked but not yet credited

items.label: Bank-only items
items.detail: Charges, interest, direct debits not yet recorded

items.label: Arrive at cash book balance
items.detail: The two records should now agree

scenes.heading: Worked example: 31 March 2025
scenes.narration: Here the bank shows twelve thousand four hundred and fifty pounds. Add the two thousand pound lodgement, take off one thousand eight hundred of unpresented cheques, and you get twelve thousand six hundred and fifty pounds.

items.label: Bank statement balance
items.detail: Closing balance at 31 March 2025

items.label: Add: lodgement 31/3
items.detail: Banked on 31 March, not yet credited

items.label: Less: unpresented cheques
items.detail: Cheques 241, 243 and 244

items.label: Adjusted bank balance
items.detail: Matches cash book per ledger: difference nil

scenes.heading: What to do with the result
scenes.narration: With a nil difference you post nothing, because the items will clear next period. If the balances still differ after adjustments, you must investigate.

items.label: Difference is nil
items.detail: Post nothing; items clear next period

items.label: Balances still differ
items.detail: Investigate the difference

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Cloud bank feeds automate much of this, but you must understand the discipline. Bank reconciliation is the cornerstone control, so never sign off accounts without one.

scenes.heading: The principal source documents
scenes.subheading: Who creates each document and where it gets posted
scenes.narration: Every entry in the books starts with a source document. In this section we'll see who creates each one and exactly where it gets posted, so your records always have evidence behind them.

scenes.heading: Sales and purchase documents
scenes.narration: Sales invoices go from you to the customer, into the sales day book, then the sales account and trade debtors. Purchase invoices come from suppliers, through the purchase day book, to expense or asset and trade creditors.

items.label: Sales invoice
items.detail: Sales day book → Sales account + Trade Debtors

items.label: Sales credit note
items.detail: Your business to customer → Sales returns day book

items.label: Purchase invoice
items.detail: Purchase day book → Expense/Asset + Trade Creditors

items.label: Purchase credit note
items.detail: Supplier to you → Purchase returns day book

scenes.heading: Bank and cash documents
scenes.narration: Bank statements come from the bank, while cheque counterfoils and paying-in slips are internal, and both go into the cash book. Petty cash vouchers are internal too, posted to the petty cash book.

items.label: Cash book
items.detail: Bank statement; cheque counterfoil or paying-in slip

items.label: Petty cash book
items.detail: Petty cash voucher, created internally

scenes.heading: Staff, payroll and finance documents
scenes.narration: Expense claims with receipts go to the expense ledger or director's loan. Payroll summaries feed the wages journal. Loan and hire purchase or lease agreements from lenders set up the creditor, interest and asset cost.

items.label: Expense claim + receipts
items.detail: Employee to company → Expense ledger or Director's Loan

items.label: Payroll summary
items.detail: From payroll software → Wages journal

items.label: Loan agreement
items.detail: From lender → Loan account + interest expense

items.label: HP / lease agreement
items.detail: From lender → HP/Lease creditor + asset cost

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: know who originates each document and where it lands. Get that right and every posting has a clear trail back to its evidence.

scenes.heading: What makes a UK VAT invoice valid?
scenes.subheading: The details an invoice needs before input VAT can be recovered
scenes.narration: To recover input VAT, you need a valid VAT invoice from your supplier. Let's look at exactly what that invoice has to show.

scenes.heading: Full invoice: who and when
scenes.narration: Under regulation 14 of the VAT Regulations 1995, a full VAT invoice starts with a sequential number, the date of issue, the tax point, and both parties' details.

items.label: Sequential number
items.detail: Each invoice carries the next number in sequence

items.label: Date and tax point
items.detail: Date of issue plus the tax point, the time of supply

items.label: Supplier details
items.detail: Name, address and VAT registration number

items.label: Customer details
items.detail: Customer's name and address

scenes.heading: Full invoice: what and how much
scenes.narration: It must then describe the supply clearly enough to identify it, and show the figures, from quantity and unit price through to the gross amount payable.

items.label: Description and quantity
items.detail: Enough to identify the goods or services, and the extent

items.label: Unit price
items.detail: Shown where applicable

items.label: Net amount
items.detail: The value before VAT

items.label: VAT rates and amounts
items.detail: Amount per rate, plus total VAT charged

items.label: Gross amount payable
items.detail: The total the customer must pay

scenes.heading: Simplified VAT invoice
scenes.narration: For retail supplies under £250 including VAT, a simplified invoice is allowed. It needs fewer fields, but some details are still essential.

items.label: When it can be used
items.detail: Retail supplies under £250 including VAT

items.label: What it must show
items.detail: Supplier name, VAT number, date, description, rate, gross

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: no valid invoice, no input VAT recovery. Check every field against regulation 14 before you claim.

scenes.heading: Retention periods
scenes.subheading: How long UK law says you must keep each type of record
scenes.narration: In this section we look at how long different records must be kept. Each rule comes from a different law, so knowing them protects you and your clients if records are ever challenged.

scenes.heading: Tax records
scenes.narration: Self-employed records are kept for five years from the thirty-first of January following the tax year. Company tax records are six years from the end of the accounting period, and VAT records six years, or ten under the capital goods scheme.

items.label: Self-employed records
items.detail: From 31 January following tax year. TMA 1970 s.12B

items.label: Company tax records
items.detail: From end of accounting period. FA 1998 Sch.18 para.21

items.label: VAT records
items.detail: 10 years for capital goods scheme. VATA 1994 Sch.11 para.6

scenes.heading: Companies Act records
scenes.narration: Under section 388 of the Companies Act 2006, private companies keep their records for three years, while public companies must keep them for six years.

scenes.heading: Payroll, pensions and anti-money laundering
scenes.narration: Payroll records are kept three years from the end of the tax year, or six for anti-money laundering purposes if you are an agent. Auto-enrolment records need six years, opt-out notices four, and anti-money laundering client records five years after the relationship ends.

items.label: Payroll records
items.detail: From end of tax year; 6 years for AML if an agent

items.label: Auto-enrolment records
items.detail: 4 years for opt-out notices. Pensions Act 2008

items.label: AML client records
items.detail: From end of business relationship. MLR 2017 reg.40

scenes.heading: Practical advice: default to 7
scenes.narration: The practical answer is to keep everything for seven years. That covers every rule we have seen and lines up with the six-year limit for contractual claims under the Limitation Act 1980, and cloud storage is near-free.

items.label: Safe default retention
items.detail: Covers all the statutory periods above

items.label: Contractual claims limit
items.detail: Limitation Act 1980

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember the main periods for each type of record, and when in doubt, keep everything for seven years.

scenes.heading: MTD digital records rules
scenes.subheading: Why every step from source to filed return must be digitally linked
scenes.narration: Under Making Tax Digital for VAT, and from 2026 for Income Tax Self Assessment, records must be kept digitally. Let's see what that means and why one retyped number can make a business non-compliant.

scenes.heading: Permitted digital links
scenes.narration: These are the permitted digital links. API connections, where software like Xero or QuickBooks Online talks directly, are the gold standard, but CSV files, emailed spreadsheets that are imported, and linked cells all count.

items.label: API connections
items.detail: Gold standard: Xero, QBO and others talk directly

items.label: CSV import and export
items.detail: Data moved between systems as CSV files

items.label: Emailed XLS or XLSX files
items.detail: Allowed if the data is imported, not retyped

items.label: Linked spreadsheet cells
items.detail: Cell A1 in sheet 1 equals A1 in sheet 2

scenes.heading: What breaks the digital link
scenes.narration: Manual re-typing between two systems breaks the digital link and is non-compliant. So is pasting values, which loses the formulas, or typing up a paper printout into a spreadsheet.

items.label: Rekeying numbers
items.detail: Manual re-typing between two systems

items.label: Copy-paste of values
items.detail: Formulas are lost, so the chain breaks

items.label: Transcribing paper
items.detail: Typing a printout into a spreadsheet

scenes.heading: Module 6 key takeaways
scenes.narration: To wrap up Module 6: regulation 14 invoice rules decide input tax recovery, keep records for the right period, and under Making Tax Digital keep digital links throughout, because copy-paste breaks the chain.

scenes.heading: Cash vs Accruals: The Two Bases
scenes.subheading: When do income and expenses count? It depends on the basis you use
scenes.narration: In this section we define the two bases for recognising income and expenses. Getting this right decides which period every transaction lands in, so it shapes the whole set of accounts.

scenes.heading: When Is It Recognised?
scenes.narration: Under the cash basis, income counts when cash is received and expenses when they're paid. Under the accruals basis, income counts when earned and expenses when incurred, whatever happens to the cash.

items.label: Cash basis
items.detail: Income when cash received; expenses when paid

items.label: Accruals basis
items.detail: Income when earned; expenses when incurred

scenes.heading: What Each Basis Involves
scenes.narration: The cash basis has no debtors, creditors, accruals or prepayments, which makes it easier for the smallest businesses. The accruals basis ties recognition to invoices raised and received, regardless of cash flow.

items.label: Cash: no adjustments
items.detail: No debtors, creditors, accruals or prepayments

items.label: Cash: simpler
items.detail: Easier for the smallest businesses

items.label: Accruals: income
items.detail: Earned when the invoice is raised

items.label: Accruals: expenses
items.detail: Incurred when the invoice is received

scenes.heading: Where Accruals Is Required
scenes.narration: The accruals basis, also called the traditional basis, is the standard required by FRS 102 and FRS 105 for company accounts. It's also the default for income tax for businesses above the cash basis threshold.

items.label: Company accounts standard
items.detail: Accruals basis required, as under FRS 105

items.label: Income tax default
items.detail: For businesses above the cash basis threshold

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: cash basis follows the money, accruals basis follows the invoices. Accruals is the standard for company accounts and the income tax default above the cash basis threshold.

scenes.heading: Cash basis: who can use it?
scenes.subheading: How eligibility changed from 6 April 2024 and who is excluded
scenes.narration: In this section we look at who can use the cash basis. The rules changed significantly in 2024, so it's vital you know both the old and the new position.

scenes.heading: Before and after 6 April 2024
scenes.narration: Until 5 April 2024, sole traders and partnerships could opt in with turnover up to £150,000 and had to leave at £300,000. From 6 April 2024, cash basis is the default and you must elect out to use accruals.

items.label: Until 5 April 2024
items.detail: Opt in up to £150,000 turnover; leave at £300,000

items.label: From 6 April 2024
items.detail: All unincorporated businesses; elect out for accruals

scenes.heading: Turnover thresholds abolished
scenes.narration: The Spring Budget 2024 also scrapped the turnover thresholds entirely, so the old £150,000 entry and £300,000 exit limits no longer apply. It's a major change.

items.label: Old entry threshold
items.detail: Abolished from 6 April 2024

items.label: Old exit threshold
items.detail: Abolished from 6 April 2024

scenes.heading: Who cannot use the cash basis
scenes.narration: Some businesses are excluded. Limited companies must use accruals under the Financial Reporting Standards, and so must limited liability partnerships and partnerships with a corporate partner.

items.label: Limited companies
items.detail: Must use accruals under FRS

items.label: LLPs
items.detail: Limited liability partnerships are excluded

items.label: Corporate partner
items.detail: Partnerships with a company as partner

scenes.heading: Other excluded taxpayers
scenes.narration: The exclusion list also covers farms using the herd basis, ministers of religion, managed service companies and Lloyd's underwriters.

items.label: Herd basis farms
items.detail: Farms that use the herd basis

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: cash basis is now the default for unincorporated businesses, thresholds are gone, and certain businesses can never use it.

scenes.heading: Cash vs accruals in practice
scenes.subheading: How six common items are treated differently under each basis
scenes.narration: Let's see how the cash basis and the accruals basis treat the same items differently at year-end. These differences change both profit and tax, so they really matter.

scenes.heading: Unpaid invoices at year-end
scenes.narration: Under the cash basis, unpaid sales and supplier invoices are ignored until money moves. Under accruals, they are recognised now, creating a debtor or a creditor.

items.label: Cash basis
items.detail: Unpaid sales not income; unpaid bills not expense yet

items.label: Accruals basis
items.detail: Income with a debtor; expense with a creditor

scenes.heading: Stock and capital spending
scenes.narration: On the cash basis, stock is generally not adjusted and capital items are expensed when paid, with capital allowances for cars only. Under accruals, closing stock is an asset and assets are capitalised and depreciated.

items.label: Stock: cash basis
items.detail: Generally not adjusted; purchases expensed when paid

items.label: Stock: accruals basis
items.detail: Closing stock asset; reduces cost of sales

items.label: Capital: cash basis
items.detail: Allowances for cars only; others expensed when paid

items.label: Capital: accruals basis
items.detail: Capitalised; depreciation in P&L, allowances for tax

scenes.heading: Loan interest and losses
scenes.narration: The cash basis caps loan interest relief at five hundred pounds a year and only lets losses be carried forward. Accruals allows full interest relief and sideways loss relief under section 64 of the Income Tax Act 2007.

items.label: Cash basis interest cap
items.detail: Maximum loan interest deduction per year

items.label: Cash basis losses
items.detail: Carried forward only; no sideways relief

items.label: Accruals losses
items.detail: Sideways relief available under ITA 2007

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: cash basis waits for money to move and has some tighter tax rules, while accruals matches items to the period with fuller reliefs.

scenes.heading: Transition adjustments
scenes.subheading: Switching between cash and accruals without double-counting
scenes.narration: When a business moves from cash to accruals, or back again, a transition adjustment is needed. It stops income and expenses being counted twice, or not at all, across the changeover.

scenes.heading: Why an adjustment is needed
scenes.narration: Without an adjustment, items can fall through the gap or be counted twice. The rules sit in the Income Tax, Trading and Other Income Act 2005, sections 232 to 240.

items.label: Double-counting
items.detail: Income or expenses taxed in both periods

items.label: Non-counting
items.detail: Income or expenses never taxed at all

scenes.heading: Worked Example 7.1
scenes.narration: Here a sole trader uses the cash basis in Year 1, then accruals in Year 2. At the end of Year 1, some customer and supplier invoices were still unpaid.

items.label: Year 1: cash basis
items.detail: Sales received in the year

items.label: Unpaid sales invoices
items.detail: Owed by customers at end of Year 1

items.label: Unpaid supplier invoices
items.detail: Owed to suppliers at end of Year 1

items.label: Year 2: accruals basis
items.detail: Transition adjustment needed

scenes.heading: The Year 2 adjustment
scenes.narration: The £8,000 of debtors is added to income, as it would never have been counted under cash, and £3,000 of creditors to expenses. So £5,000 is added to taxable profit, spread over 6 years if on transition to MTD ITSA.

items.label: Added to income
items.detail: Debtors created on the transition date

items.label: Added to expenses
items.detail: Creditors created on the transition date

items.label: Net added to profit
items.detail: Spread over 6 years if on transition to MTD ITSA

scenes.heading: Module 7 key takeaways
scenes.narration: To sum up Module 7: cash basis is now the default for unincorporated businesses, companies must use accruals, and transition adjustments prevent double-counting when the basis changes.

scenes.heading: What Dext is and why we use it
scenes.subheading: Document capture and pre-accounting, from source document to ledger
scenes.narration: Dext, formerly Receipt Bank, is a document-capture and pre-accounting platform owned by HG Capital. Let's see what it does and why practices rely on it.

scenes.subheading: How the Practice account sits above each client workspace, and how to add a client
scenes.narration: In this section we look at how a Dext Practice account sits above your client accounts, and the steps for adding a new client properly from day one.

items.label: Client workspace

scenes.heading: Processing items in the Inbox
scenes.subheading: How to check, code and speed up items in Dext's Costs and Sales Inbox
scenes.narration: In this section we look at what happens when an item lands in your Dext Inbox, how you check it, and how rules and line splitting save you time while keeping the books accurate.

scenes.heading: What Dext extracts
scenes.narration: When an item arrives in the Costs or Sales Inbox, Dext pulls out the supplier, date, total, VAT and currency. With the line-item add-on, it captures the individual lines too.

scenes.heading: What is VAT, conceptually?
scenes.subheading: A multi-stage tax on the value added at each link of a supply chain
scenes.narration: Welcome to VAT fundamentals. Before we tackle registration, rates and returns, let's get clear on what VAT actually is and who really bears the cost.

scenes.heading: How VAT flows through a business
scenes.narration: Each VAT-registered business charges output VAT on its sales, recovers input VAT on its purchases, and pays the net difference to HMRC, which is His Majesty's Revenue and Customs.

items.label: Charge output VAT
items.detail: Added to the business's sales

items.label: Recover input VAT
items.detail: Reclaimed on the business's purchases

items.label: Pay the net to HMRC
items.detail: Output VAT less input VAT

scenes.heading: Who really bears the cost?
scenes.narration: The economic burden falls on the final consumer who isn't VAT-registered. The businesses in between are tax collectors, not taxpayers, on each transaction.

items.label: Intermediate businesses
items.detail: Collect VAT and pass the net to HMRC

items.label: Final consumer
items.detail: Not VAT-registered, so cannot recover VAT

scenes.heading: Where the VAT rules come from
scenes.narration: The law is the Value Added Tax Act 1994, backed by the VAT Regulations 1995. HMRC's Notice 700 series helps interpret the rules, but remember, those notices are not law.

items.label: VATA 1994
items.detail: Value Added Tax Act 1994

items.label: HMRC Notice 700 series
items.detail: Interpretation only, not law

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So, VAT taxes value added at every stage, businesses collect it, consumers bear it, and the Act and Regulations are the law while HMRC notices simply interpret it.

scenes.heading: The four UK VAT rates
scenes.subheading: Standard, reduced, zero-rated and exempt, plus out of scope supplies
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the four UK VAT rates. Knowing which applies decides what VAT you charge and, crucially, whether you can recover VAT on your costs.

scenes.heading: Four rates at a glance
scenes.narration: Twenty percent is the default for almost everything. Five percent covers listed supplies like domestic energy. Zero rate covers most food and books, and exempt covers things like insurance and finance.

items.label: Standard
items.detail: Most goods and services, restaurant meals, adult clothing

items.label: Reduced (VATA Sch 7A)
items.detail: Domestic gas and electricity, children's car seats

items.label: Zero-rated (VATA Sch 8)
items.detail: Most food, books, children's clothing, new-build homes

items.label: Exempt (VATA Sch 9)
items.detail: Insurance, most finance, education, health, postal

scenes.heading: Zero-rated vs exempt
scenes.narration: Both charge nothing on the sale, but zero-rated sales are taxable, so input VAT is fully recoverable. Exempt sales are not taxable, so input VAT is blocked, subject to partial exemption in Module 18.

items.label: Zero-rated
items.detail: Taxable supply: input VAT fully recoverable

items.label: Exempt
items.detail: Non-taxable supply: input VAT blocked

scenes.heading: Two VAT-registered businesses
scenes.narration: Picture two registered businesses. The insurance broker recovers no input VAT on its overheads, while the children's clothing retailer recovers all of it.

items.label: Insurance broker
items.detail: Exempt sales, so no input VAT recovered on overheads

items.label: Children's clothes shop
items.detail: Zero-rated sales, so all input VAT recovered

scenes.heading: Out of scope supplies
scenes.narration: Out of scope is separate: the supply is made overseas, or isn't a supply at all, like wages or dividends. These usually stay out of Box 6, though reverse-charged cross-border services to UK businesses can go in.

items.label: Place of supply overseas
items.detail: The supply is not made in the UK

items.label: Not a supply for VAT
items.detail: Wages, dividends, statutory fines

items.label: Box 6 of VAT return
items.detail: Usually excluded; reverse-charged services can appear

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Keep these points in mind, especially the difference between zero-rated and exempt, as it drives input VAT recovery.

scenes.heading: VAT Registration
scenes.subheading: When you must register, when you may deregister, and voluntary registration
scenes.narration: In this section we look at when a business must register for VAT, when it can deregister, and when it can choose to register. Getting the dates right matters, because it decides when VAT must be charged.

scenes.heading: Compulsory registration: two tests
scenes.narration: For 2024 to 25 the threshold is ninety thousand pounds of taxable turnover over a rolling twelve months, up from eighty-five thousand on 1 April 2024. Two tests apply: one looks back, one looks forward.

items.label: Threshold
items.detail: Rolling 12 months; was £85,000 before 1 April 2024

items.label: Historic test
items.detail: At any month end, prior 12 months exceed £90,000

items.label: Historic: deadline
items.detail: Must register within 30 days of the breach

items.label: Future test
items.detail: Expect over £90,000 in next 30 days alone; effective at start

scenes.heading: Deregistration threshold
scenes.narration: The deregistration threshold is eighty-eight thousand pounds, up from eighty-three thousand on 1 April 2024. A business can choose to deregister if it reasonably expects taxable turnover in the next twelve months to be below that.

items.label: Deregistration threshold
items.detail: Raised from £83,000 on 1 April 2024

items.label: Test period
items.detail: Expected taxable turnover over the next 12 months

scenes.heading: Voluntary registration
scenes.narration: Any business can register voluntarily, whatever its turnover, including those making zero-rated supplies, which often benefit because they can recover input VAT. But a business making only exempt supplies cannot register.

items.label: Available
items.detail: Any turnover, including zero-rated suppliers recovering input VAT

items.label: Not available
items.detail: Businesses making only exempt supplies

scenes.heading: Worked example: registration date
scenes.narration: A consultancy goes over ninety thousand pounds on 18 May 2025 after one big invoice. It must notify HMRC by 30 June, and from 1 July 2025 it must charge output VAT on all standard-rated sales.

items.label: Crosses £90,000
items.detail: One big invoice tips it over; breach at end of May

items.label: Notify HMRC by
items.detail: Within 30 days of the end of the breach month

items.label: Effective date
items.detail: Registration takes effect

items.label: Charge output VAT
items.detail: On all standard-rated sales

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember the two thresholds, the historic and future tests, the thirty day deadline, and who can register voluntarily.

scenes.heading: The Tax Point
scenes.subheading: The date a supply counts as made for VAT, and which return it falls into
scenes.narration: Welcome to the tax point. It's the date a supply is treated as made for VAT purposes, and it matters because it decides which VAT return the supply belongs in.

scenes.heading: Basic tax points by supply
scenes.narration: The basic tax point depends on the type of supply. Goods count when removed or made available, services when performed, and continuous services at the end of each period covered by an invoice.

items.label: Goods
items.detail: When removed or made available to the customer

items.label: Services
items.detail: When the service is performed

items.label: Continuous services
items.detail: End of each period covered by an invoice

items.label: Sale or return goods
items.detail: Earlier of adoption by customer or 12 months from removal

scenes.heading: Actual tax point overrides
scenes.narration: For goods and services, an actual tax point can override the basic one. If an invoice is issued or payment received first, the earlier of those applies; an invoice within 14 days of the basic tax point also becomes the tax point.

items.label: Find the basic tax point
items.detail: Removal of goods or performance of service

items.label: Invoice or payment earlier?
items.detail: The earlier of the two becomes the actual tax point

items.label: Invoice within 14 days?
items.detail: The invoice date becomes the actual tax point

scenes.heading: Continuous supplies vs sale or return
scenes.narration: For continuous services, the tax point is the earlier of invoice issued or payment received. For goods on sale or return, it's when the customer adopts the goods, or 12 months from removal if sooner.

items.label: Continuous services
items.detail: Earlier of invoice issued or payment received

items.label: Sale or return
items.detail: Earlier of customer adopting goods or 12 months

scenes.heading: The 14-day rule
scenes.narration: Most businesses invoice within 14 days, so in practice the invoice date is usually the tax point. Invoice later than that, and the basic tax point applies, unless H M R C agrees a longer period.

items.label: Basic tax point
items.detail: Goods removed or service performed

items.label: Invoice within 14 days
items.detail: Invoice date becomes the actual tax point

items.label: Invoice after 14 days
items.detail: Basic tax point applies unless HMRC agrees longer

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: the tax point decides the VAT return, basic tax points vary by supply, earlier invoices or payments override them, and the 14-day rule usually makes the invoice date the tax point.

scenes.heading: The 9-box VAT return
scenes.subheading: What each box holds and how the boxes link to give the VAT due to HMRC
scenes.narration: Every VAT return is built from nine boxes. Let's walk through what goes in each one, so you can complete and check a return with confidence.

scenes.heading: Boxes 1 to 3: VAT due
scenes.narration: Box 1 is the output VAT you've charged on sales. Box 2 is VAT on acquisitions from EU member states, now Northern Ireland only after Brexit. Box 3 simply adds the two together.

items.label: Box 1
items.detail: VAT due on sales and other outputs

items.label: Box 2
items.detail: VAT on EU acquisitions, now NI-only post-Brexit

items.label: Box 3
items.detail: Total VAT due

scenes.heading: Boxes 4 and 5: net VAT
scenes.narration: Box 4 is the input VAT you can reclaim on purchases. Box 5 takes Box 3 minus Box 4: if positive you pay HMRC, if negative you get a repayment.

items.label: Box 4: input VAT
items.detail: VAT reclaimed on purchases and other inputs

items.label: Box 5: Box 3 − Box 4
items.detail: Net VAT due to HMRC

items.label: Positive or negative?
items.detail: Positive is payable; negative is a repayment

scenes.heading: Boxes 6 and 7: net values
scenes.narration: Boxes 6 and 7 record values, not VAT. Box 6 is total sales and outputs, Box 7 total purchases and inputs, both excluding any VAT.

items.label: Box 6: sales
items.detail: Total value of sales and all other outputs

items.label: Box 7: purchases
items.detail: Total value of purchases and all other inputs

scenes.heading: Boxes 8 and 9: EU goods
scenes.narration: Box 8 is the value of goods dispatched to EU member states, and Box 9 the value of goods acquired from them. After Brexit, both apply to Northern Ireland only.

items.label: Box 8: dispatches
items.detail: Total value of goods dispatched to EU member states

items.label: Box 9: acquisitions
items.detail: Total value of goods acquired from EU member states

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: Boxes 1 to 5 deal with VAT itself, Boxes 6 to 9 with net values, and Box 5 tells you whether you pay or get money back.

scenes.heading: VAT filing and payment deadlines
scenes.subheading: When VAT returns are due and when the tax must be paid
scenes.narration: In this section we look at when VAT returns must be filed and when the VAT must be paid. Getting these dates right keeps your clients compliant.

scenes.heading: The one month and seven days rule
scenes.narration: For quarterly returns, filing and payment are both due one month and seven days after the quarter ends. So a quarter ending 31 March is due by 7 May.

items.label: VAT quarter ends
items.detail: End of the VAT period

items.label: Return and payment due
items.detail: One month and seven days later

scenes.heading: Ways VAT returns are made
scenes.narration: Monthly returns follow the same one month and seven days rule, and are used by repayment traders. The Annual Accounting Scheme means one return a year plus nine monthly payments on account, covered in Module 14.

items.label: Quarterly returns
items.detail: Filing and payment after quarter end

items.label: Monthly returns
items.detail: Same rule; used by repayment traders

items.label: Annual Accounting Scheme
items.detail: Plus 9 monthly payments on account

scenes.narration: Businesses with turnover over £2.3 million fall into the Payments on Account regime. They make monthly payments on account based on the previous year's VAT liability.

items.detail: Brings a business into the regime

items.label: Monthly payments on account
items.detail: Based on the prior year's liability
