scenes.narration: So remember: one month and seven days for quarterly and monthly returns, one return and nine payments under annual accounting, and monthly payments on account above £2.3 million.

scenes.heading: Output and input VAT basics
scenes.subheading: Calculating VAT on sales and knowing when VAT on costs can be recovered
scenes.narration: In this section we work out output VAT on sales, then look at when a business can recover input VAT on its costs, and which input VAT is blocked. Get this right and your VAT returns will stand up.

scenes.heading: Working out output VAT
scenes.narration: On a VAT-exclusive price, simply multiply by the rate. On a VAT-inclusive price, multiply by rate over one plus rate, which at the standard rate is twenty over one hundred and twenty, or one sixth.

items.label: VAT-exclusive price
items.detail: Apply the rate directly to the net price

items.label: VAT-inclusive price
items.detail: Price × rate ÷ (1 + rate); standard rate is 20/120

scenes.heading: Four conditions to recover input VAT
scenes.narration: Input VAT is only recoverable when all four conditions are met. Note the invoice rule: an HMRC-accepted alternative works for amounts below twenty-five pounds, or import documentation.

scenes.heading: Blocked input VAT
scenes.narration: Some input VAT is blocked. Car purchases are usually blocked unless used exclusively for business, UK client entertainment is fully blocked, private use is apportioned, and Margin Scheme goods are blocked.

items.label: Cars (purchase)
items.detail: Exception only for taxis, driving schools, car hire

items.label: UK client entertainment
items.detail: Fully blocked; staff entertaining is recoverable

items.label: Private or exempt use
items.detail: Exempt supplies follow partial exemption, Module 18

items.label: Margin Scheme goods
items.detail: Input VAT on the goods themselves is blocked

scenes.heading: Module 13 key takeaways
scenes.narration: To wrap up Module 13: four rates plus outside the scope, a ninety thousand pound registration threshold, tax point rules, the nine-box return due one month and seven days after quarter end, and the input VAT rules.

items.label: Know basic and actual tax point

scenes.heading: Standard Accounting Scheme
scenes.subheading: The default VAT scheme, based on tax points rather than cash
scenes.narration: Let's start with the standard accounting scheme, also called the accruals scheme. It's the default way businesses account for VAT, so you need to know it well.

scenes.heading: When VAT Is Accounted For
scenes.narration: Output VAT on sales is accounted for at the tax point of the sale, typically the invoice date. Input VAT on purchases is recovered at the tax point of the purchase.

items.label: Output VAT on sales
items.detail: Due at the sale's tax point, typically invoice date

items.label: Input VAT on purchases
items.detail: Recovered at the purchase's tax point

scenes.heading: The Cashflow Burden
scenes.narration: Because VAT follows the invoice, not the payment, VAT can be due on a sale before the customer has paid. That's a real cashflow burden for businesses with long debtor days.

items.label: VAT due before payment
items.detail: Owed on the invoice even if the customer hasn't paid

items.label: Long debtor days
items.detail: Slow-paying customers make the burden worse

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: standard accounting is the default, it works on tax points, and it can strain cashflow when customers pay slowly.

items.label: Output VAT at sale tax point

scenes.heading: Cash Accounting Scheme
scenes.subheading: Account for VAT when cash actually moves, not when invoices are raised
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the Cash Accounting Scheme, which ties your VAT to when money is actually paid and received. It matters because it solves a real cashflow problem for smaller businesses.

scenes.heading: When VAT Is Accounted For
scenes.narration: Under this scheme, output VAT is due only when your customer pays you, and input VAT is recoverable only when you pay your supplier. So you never pay over VAT you have not yet collected.

items.label: Output VAT
items.detail: Due when payment is received from the customer

items.label: Input VAT
items.detail: Recoverable when you pay the supplier

scenes.heading: Eligibility Thresholds
scenes.narration: You can join if your taxable turnover is one point three five million pounds or less. You must leave once it goes above one point six million pounds.

items.label: Join the scheme
items.detail: Taxable turnover at or below this to enter

items.label: Must leave
items.detail: Leave when taxable turnover exceeds this

scenes.heading: Where It Cannot Be Used
scenes.narration: The scheme is available to most businesses, but not for imports, not for acquisitions from the EU involving Northern Ireland, and not for supplies more than six months overdue from the supplier.

items.label: Imports
items.detail: Excluded from cash accounting

items.label: NI and EU acquisitions
items.detail: Acquisitions from the EU into Northern Ireland excluded

items.label: Overdue supplies
items.detail: Supplies over 6 months overdue from supplier excluded

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: VAT follows the cash, the scheme helps cashflow, the entry and exit thresholds differ, and some transactions are always excluded.

items.label: Output VAT when paid to you

scenes.heading: The Annual Accounting Scheme
scenes.subheading: One VAT return a year, with interim payments spread across the year
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the Annual Accounting Scheme, which lets a business file just one VAT return a year and spread its payments, making cash flow and admin far more predictable.

scenes.heading: How the scheme works
scenes.narration: Interim payments are based on last year's VAT liability, paid either nine times monthly or three times quarterly. Then the single annual return goes in with a final balancing payment.

items.label: Use prior-year liability
items.detail: Interim payments are based on last year's VAT

items.label: Make interim payments
items.detail: 9 monthly or 3 quarterly payments

items.label: Submit one annual return
items.detail: A single VAT return for the whole year

items.label: Pay the balance
items.detail: Final balancing payment goes with the return

scenes.heading: Scheme thresholds
scenes.narration: The same thresholds apply as in the scheme we have just covered: one point three five million pounds and one point six million pounds.

items.label: First threshold
items.detail: Same figure as the previous scheme

items.label: Second threshold
items.detail: Same figure as the previous scheme

scenes.heading: Combining schemes
scenes.narration: A business can use Annual Accounting together with Cash Accounting, so it can enjoy fewer returns and still account for VAT when cash actually changes hands.

items.label: Annual Accounting
items.detail: One return a year with interim payments

items.label: Cash Accounting
items.detail: Can be combined with Annual Accounting

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: one annual return, interim payments based on last year, a final balancing payment, the same thresholds, and it can be combined with Cash Accounting.

scenes.heading: The Flat Rate Scheme
scenes.subheading: Charge standard VAT, pay HMRC a fixed percentage of turnover
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the Flat Rate Scheme, a simpler way for small businesses to account for VAT, and the anti-abuse rule that can wipe out its benefit.

scenes.heading: How the scheme works
scenes.narration: You still charge customers VAT at standard rates, but you pay HMRC a fixed flat-rate percentage of your VAT-inclusive turnover. You generally cannot reclaim input VAT, except on capital assets over £2,000 including VAT in a single transaction.

items.label: Output VAT
items.detail: Charge customers VAT at standard rates

items.label: Pay HMRC
items.detail: Fixed percentage of VAT-inclusive turnover

items.label: Input VAT
items.detail: Except capital assets over £2,000 incl. VAT

scenes.heading: Key scheme limits
scenes.narration: You can join if turnover excluding VAT will be £150,000 or less in the next twelve months, and must leave once VAT-inclusive turnover exceeds £230,000. In your first year you get one percent off the published rate.

items.label: Entry threshold
items.detail: Turnover excl. VAT in next 12 months

items.label: Exit threshold
items.detail: VAT-inclusive turnover

items.label: First-year discount
items.detail: Off the published flat rate

scenes.heading: Limited Cost Trader rule
scenes.narration: If your goods cost less than two percent of VAT-inclusive turnover, or less than £1,000 a year, you are a Limited Cost Trader and pay a punitive 16.5 percent rate. This effectively removes the benefit for labour-only consultancies.

items.label: Goods under 2% or £1,000
items.detail: Punitive flat rate for Limited Cost Traders

scenes.heading: Worked example: IT consultant
scenes.narration: An IT consultant turns over £80,000 plus VAT, so £96,000 inclusive, and spends just £200 on goods, below £1,920. Paying 16.5 percent leaves only £160, against about £40 under standard accounting, so the benefit is marginal.

items.label: Turnover incl. VAT
items.detail: £80,000 plus £16,000 output VAT

items.label: Goods spend
items.detail: Below 2% of £96,000, which is £1,920: LCT applies

items.label: Net retained
items.detail: Vs about £40 under standard: marginal

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Remember the entry and exit limits, the first-year discount, the capital asset exception, and always test for Limited Cost Trader status before recommending the scheme.

scenes.heading: Margin Schemes
scenes.subheading: How dealers in second-hand goods account for VAT on their margin
scenes.narration: In this section we look at margin schemes, a special way of accounting for VAT used by dealers who buy and resell goods.

scenes.heading: Who uses a margin scheme?
scenes.narration: Margin schemes are for dealers in second-hand goods, antiques, art and used cars.

scenes.heading: How the VAT is worked out
scenes.narration: Rather than charging VAT on the full selling price, the dealer calculates VAT on their margin, which is the sale price minus the purchase price.

items.label: Take the sale price
items.detail: What the dealer sells the item for

items.label: Deduct purchase price
items.detail: What the dealer paid for the item

items.label: VAT on the margin
items.detail: VAT is calculated on the difference only

scenes.heading: No input VAT recovery
scenes.narration: One important catch: under a margin scheme, the dealer cannot recover input VAT on the goods they buy.

items.label: Input VAT on goods
items.detail: Cannot be recovered under a margin scheme

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: margin schemes suit dealers in second-hand goods, VAT is charged on the margin, and input VAT on the goods cannot be recovered.

scenes.heading: TOMS: Tour Operators' Margin Scheme
scenes.subheading: A compulsory VAT scheme for businesses reselling travel as packages
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the Tour Operators' Margin Scheme, usually called TOMS. It's a specialist VAT scheme you need to recognise, because it's compulsory for the businesses it covers.

scenes.heading: What gets bundled and resold
scenes.narration: TOMS applies to businesses that buy in travel, accommodation or passenger transport, then resell it bundled together as a package.

items.label: Travel
items.detail: Bought in from other suppliers

items.label: Accommodation
items.detail: Bought in from other suppliers

items.label: Passenger transport
items.detail: Bought in from other suppliers

items.label: Sold as a package
items.detail: Resold to customers as one bundle

scenes.heading: How VAT is charged
scenes.narration: Under TOMS, VAT is charged on the margin, not the full selling price. And for businesses that fit the description, using the scheme is mandatory, not optional.

items.label: VAT basis
items.detail: VAT is due on the margin, not the full price

items.label: Is it optional?
items.detail: Required for businesses that fit the scheme

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: TOMS is compulsory for package travel resellers, VAT is charged on the margin, and it's a specialist sector worth flagging when you meet it.

scenes.heading: Retail Schemes
scenes.subheading: How shops with mostly cash sales to consumers can account for VAT
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the VAT retail schemes. They matter because they let shops account for VAT without issuing a VAT invoice for every single sale.

scenes.heading: Three retail scheme variants
scenes.narration: There are three variants. Point of sale suits shops with modern electronic tills, apportionment splits mixed-rate till takings, and then there is direct calculation.

items.label: Point-of-sale
items.detail: For shops with modern EPOS tills

items.label: Apportionment
items.detail: Splits mixed-rate till takings

items.label: Direct Calculation
items.detail: A third method shops can use

scenes.heading: A typical retail shop
scenes.narration: Picture a busy shop selling mainly to the public for cash. Rather than invoicing each customer, it uses a retail scheme to work out VAT on its takings.

items.label: Mostly cash sales
items.detail: Customers are consumers, not businesses

items.label: No per-sale invoices
items.detail: Issuing one for every sale would be impractical

items.label: Uses a retail scheme
items.detail: VAT is accounted for from till takings

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: retail schemes are for shops with mostly cash sales to consumers, there are three variants, and they remove the need for per-transaction VAT invoices.

scenes.heading: VAT Group Registration
scenes.subheading: Section 43 of the VAT Act: one registration for commonly controlled companies
scenes.narration: In this section we look at VAT group registration under section 43 of the Value Added Tax Act, and then recap the whole module on VAT schemes.

scenes.heading: How a VAT group works
scenes.narration: Companies under common control can form one VAT group with a single VAT registration number and one return. Supplies between members are simply ignored for VAT.

items.label: Who can join
items.detail: Bodies corporate under common control

items.label: One registration
items.detail: A single VAT registration number and one return

items.label: Internal supplies
items.detail: Supplies between group members are disregarded

scenes.heading: Risks to watch
scenes.narration: Take care with partially exempt members in the group. And remember every member is jointly and severally liable for the group's VAT.

items.label: Partially-exempt members
items.detail: Need care when included in the group

items.label: Joint and several liability
items.detail: Every member is liable for the group's VAT

scenes.heading: Module 14 recap: the schemes
scenes.narration: Cash accounting, for turnover up to 1.35 million pounds, helps cashflow when customers pay slowly. Annual accounting cuts admin with one return plus interim payments.

items.label: Cash Accounting
items.detail: Helps cashflow when customers slow-pay

items.label: Annual Accounting
items.detail: Less admin: one return plus interim payments

items.label: Flat Rate Scheme
items.detail: Limited Cost Trader rules hit labour-only firms

items.label: Margin, TOMS, Retail
items.detail: Schemes for specialised sectors

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So, a VAT group means one number, one return, internal supplies ignored and shared liability. And each scheme in this module suits a different kind of business.

scenes.heading: Domestic Supplies of Goods
scenes.subheading: Charging VAT on goods supplied within the UK
scenes.narration: Let's start with the simplest case: goods you supply within the UK. Getting the rate and the timing right here underpins everything else in this module.

scenes.heading: The Three VAT Rates
scenes.narration: You charge VAT at the appropriate rate: twenty percent, five percent or zero percent. Which one applies depends on what the goods are.

items.label: Standard rate
items.detail: The default rate for domestic supplies

items.label: Reduced rate
items.detail: Goods listed in VATA Schedule 7A

items.label: Zero rate
items.detail: Goods listed in VATA Schedule 8

scenes.heading: Where the Rates Come From
scenes.narration: The legislation is the Value Added Tax Act 1994. Schedule 8 sets out zero-rated supplies, and Schedule 7A sets out the reduced rate.

items.label: VATA Schedule 8
items.detail: Zero-rated supplies

items.label: VATA Schedule 7A
items.detail: Reduced-rate supplies

scenes.heading: Charging VAT on a Domestic Sale
scenes.narration: In practice, identify the right rate from the schedules, charge it, then apply the standard tax point rules to know when the VAT is due.

items.label: Identify the goods
items.detail: Check Schedules 8 and 7A

items.label: Fix the tax point
items.detail: Use the standard tax point rules

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: three rates, two schedules to check, and the standard tax point rules for timing.

scenes.heading: Exports of Goods: UK to Outside UK
scenes.subheading: When exported goods can be zero-rated, and the evidence you need
scenes.narration: In this section we look at goods sold from the UK to customers outside the UK. Getting the VAT right depends on one thing above all: proof that the goods really left.

scenes.heading: The Zero-Rating Rule
scenes.narration: Exports of goods are zero-rated under Schedule 8, Group 7, but only if you hold evidence that the goods were exported within three months of the supply.

items.label: VAT on exported goods
items.detail: Zero-rated under Schedule 8, Group 7

items.label: Time limit for evidence
items.detail: Export must be evidenced within 3 months of supply

scenes.heading: Acceptable Export Evidence
scenes.narration: So what counts as evidence? Shipping documents, or proof from a courier that the goods were dispatched to a destination outside the UK.

items.label: Shipping documents
items.detail: Paperwork showing the goods were shipped abroad

items.label: Courier proof of dispatch
items.detail: Confirms dispatch to a destination outside the UK

scenes.heading: No Evidence, No Zero Rate
scenes.narration: Without that evidence, the zero rate falls away and the sale must be treated as standard-rated, so always keep your export paperwork safe.

items.label: Missing export evidence
items.detail: Supply must be treated as standard-rated

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: To recap: exports are zero-rated under Schedule 8, Group 7, you need evidence within three months, and without it the sale is standard-rated.

scenes.heading: Postponed VAT Accounting
scenes.subheading: Accounting for import VAT on the VAT return rather than at the border
scenes.narration: In this section we look at postponed VAT accounting, or PVA, for imports. It lets a business deal with import VAT on its VAT return instead of paying it at the border.

scenes.heading: How PVA hits the VAT return
scenes.narration: The same import VAT goes in Box 1 as output tax and in Box 4 as input tax, subject to the normal recovery rules. Box 7 shows the net value of the imports.

items.label: Import VAT as output
items.detail: Output entry for the import VAT

items.label: Same VAT as input
items.detail: Input entry, subject to recovery

items.label: Net value of imports
items.detail: Value of goods imported, excluding VAT

scenes.heading: The cash effect
scenes.narration: Because the output and input entries cancel out, a business that can fully recover its VAT pays nothing extra in cash. That is the big advantage over paying at the border.

items.label: Goods arrive in the UK
items.detail: No import VAT paid at the border under PVA

items.label: VAT in Box 1 and Box 4
items.detail: Output and input entries of the same amount

items.label: Fully recovering business
items.detail: Net cash effect is nil

scenes.heading: Using PVA in practice
scenes.narration: PVA has been the default since 1 January 2021. To use it, tick the box on the customs declaration, then download the monthly Postponed Import VAT Statement from the Customs Declaration Service.

items.label: Tick PVA on declaration
items.detail: Select PVA on the customs declaration

items.label: Download monthly PIVS
items.detail: Postponed Import VAT Statement from CDS

items.label: Complete the VAT return
items.detail: Enter the figures in Boxes 1, 4 and 7

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: PVA is the default since 1 January 2021, import VAT goes in Boxes 1 and 4, net imports in Box 7, and the monthly statement backs up your figures.

scenes.heading: Northern Ireland Protocol: Goods
scenes.subheading: How VAT works for goods moving between GB, NI and the EU
scenes.narration: Northern Ireland has a special VAT position for goods, so you need to know which rules apply depending on where goods are moving to and from.

scenes.heading: Goods versus services
scenes.narration: Northern Ireland remains in the EU VAT system for goods only. Services are not covered by this arrangement.

items.label: Goods
items.detail: NI stays in the EU VAT system for goods

items.label: Services
items.detail: The EU VAT system for NI does not apply to services

scenes.heading: Moving goods: GB, NI and the EU
scenes.narration: Goods sent from Great Britain to Northern Ireland are generally zero-rated, with import VAT on arrival, where postponed VAT accounting is available. Between Northern Ireland and the EU, EU rules continue.

items.label: GB to NI dispatch
items.detail: Goods sent from GB to NI are generally zero-rated

items.label: Arrival in NI
items.detail: Postponed VAT accounting (PVA) is available

items.label: NI to EU dispatch
items.detail: When sent to an EU VAT-registered customer

items.label: EU to NI acquisition
items.detail: Acquisitions reported in Box 2 and Box 9

scenes.heading: Spotting an NI trader
scenes.narration: Northern Ireland traders have a VAT registration number starting with the prefix X I, which tells you the Protocol rules for goods apply.

items.label: NI VAT number prefix
items.detail: Used by Northern Ireland traders

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Let's recap the key points on the Northern Ireland Protocol before we talk them through together.

items.label: NI in EU VAT for goods only
NI and EU: EU rules apply

scenes.heading: Distance selling to EU consumers
scenes.subheading: Selling goods business to consumer into the EU, and a recap of Module 15
scenes.narration: In this section we look at selling goods directly to consumers in the European Union, then recap the key points of Module 15 on VAT on goods.

scenes.heading: Three routes for EU B2C sales
scenes.narration: There are three options: register in each EU member state where you exceed its distance-selling threshold, use the One Stop Shop through a Northern Ireland registration, or appoint a fiscal representative.

items.label: Register in each state
items.detail: Where sales exceed that state's distance-selling threshold

items.label: One Stop Shop
items.detail: Used via a Northern Ireland registration

items.label: Fiscal representative
items.detail: A representative handles VAT in the member state

scenes.heading: A specialist area
scenes.narration: This is a specialist area, so the right step is to refer the client to a VAT specialist rather than advise on it alone.

items.label: Refer to a VAT specialist
items.detail: Distance selling to the EU needs specialist advice

scenes.heading: Module 15 summary
scenes.narration: To wrap up the module: exports are zero-rated with proper evidence, imports use postponed VAT accounting, and Northern Ireland stays in EU VAT for goods.

items.label: Exports
items.detail: Zero-rated, provided proper evidence is held

items.label: Imports
items.detail: No cashflow drag for fully-recovering businesses

items.label: Northern Ireland
items.detail: Remains in EU VAT for goods; XI VAT number prefix

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Keep these points in mind: know the three routes for EU consumer sales, refer to a specialist, and remember the module's rules on exports, imports and Northern Ireland.

items.label: Register per state, OSS or rep
NI in EU VAT for goods: XI

scenes.heading: Place of Supply foundations
scenes.subheading: Where is a service treated as supplied, and is it within UK VAT?
scenes.narration: Welcome to place of supply, often shortened to POS. These rules decide where a service is treated as supplied, which tells us whether UK VAT applies at all.

scenes.heading: Why place of supply matters
scenes.narration: Here's the key principle: only supplies made in the UK are within UK VAT. So before charging VAT on a service, you first need to know where it's supplied.

items.label: Within UK VAT
items.detail: Only supplies made in the UK are within UK VAT

scenes.heading: The two general rules
scenes.narration: For business to business supplies, the place of supply is where the customer belongs. For business to consumer supplies, it's where the supplier belongs.

items.label: General B2B
items.detail: Business to business: POS is where the customer belongs

items.label: General B2C
items.detail: Business to consumer: POS is where the supplier belongs

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: only UK supplies are within UK VAT, and the general rules point to the customer for business customers and the supplier for consumers.

items.label: Only UK supplies get UK VAT

scenes.heading: Special Place of Supply Rules
scenes.subheading: Services where the place of supply follows special rules, not the general ones
scenes.narration: Some services have their own special place of supply rules. Knowing them matters, because the place of supply decides which country's VAT applies.

scenes.heading: Rules Tied to Location
scenes.narration: For land-related services, the place of supply is where the land is. For short-term hire of transport, it's where the vehicle is put at the customer's disposal.

items.label: Land-related services
items.detail: Place of supply is where the land is

items.label: Short-term transport hire
items.detail: Where vehicle is put at customer's disposal

scenes.heading: Where It Physically Happens
scenes.narration: Restaurant and catering services are supplied where they're physically performed. Cultural, artistic and sporting admissions to consumers are supplied where the event is carried out.

items.label: Restaurant & catering
items.detail: Where physically performed

items.label: Cultural, arts, sport
items.detail: Business to consumer admission: where carried out

scenes.heading: Transport and Digital Services
scenes.narration: Passenger transport is supplied where the transport takes place. Digital services to non-business EU consumers are supplied where the consumer is, using the One Stop Shop, known as OSS.

items.label: Passenger transport
items.detail: Where the transport takes place

items.label: Digital services
items.detail: To non-business EU consumers: where consumer is

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So, remember these six special rules. Each one points to a specific location that decides where VAT is due.

scenes.heading: Reverse Charge on Overseas Services
scenes.subheading: How a UK customer self-accounts for VAT on services bought from abroad
scenes.narration: When a UK business buys services from an overseas supplier, the customer accounts for the VAT itself. This is the reverse charge, and it's worth getting right on every return.

scenes.heading: Self-Accounting on the VAT Return
scenes.narration: Using a £1,000 service at 20%, the customer puts £200 in Box 1 and the same £200 in Box 4, subject to recovery. The £1,000 net value goes in both Box 6 and Box 7.

items.label: Box 1: output VAT
items.detail: VAT as if a UK supply: £1,000 × 20%

items.label: Box 4: input VAT
items.detail: Same amount, subject to recovery

items.label: Box 6: net value
items.detail: Net value of the service

items.label: Box 7: net value
items.detail: Same net value again

scenes.heading: Why the Reverse Charge Exists
scenes.narration: For a fully recovering business, the net cash effect is nil. The point of the mechanism is to stop foreign suppliers undercutting UK suppliers by avoiding UK VAT.

items.label: Fully recovering business
items.detail: Box 1 and Box 4 cancel out, so no net cash cost

items.label: Level playing field
items.detail: Foreign suppliers can't undercut UK ones by avoiding VAT

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: the UK customer self-accounts, using all four boxes, and for a fully recovering business the cash effect is nil while competition stays fair.

items.label: Box 1: VAT as if UK supply
Nil net cash if fully recovering

scenes.heading: CIS Domestic Reverse Charge
scenes.subheading: When construction VAT shifts from subcontractor to customer
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the Construction Industry Scheme domestic reverse charge, which applies from 1 March 2021. It changes who pays the VAT to HMRC on certain construction work.

scenes.heading: DRC applies when ALL are true
scenes.narration: The reverse charge only applies when all four conditions are met. If even one is missing, normal VAT rules apply instead.

scenes.heading: How the invoice and return work
scenes.narration: The subcontractor's invoice shows no VAT, just the reverse charge statement. The customer then accounts for the VAT themselves, entering it in Box 1 and Box 4 of their return.

items.label: Invoice shows no VAT
items.detail: Subcontractor charges no VAT on the invoice

items.label: Add the statement
items.detail: Reverse charge: customer to pay VAT to HMRC

items.label: Customer fills return
items.detail: Enters the VAT in Box 1 and Box 4

scenes.heading: End-user statements
scenes.narration: Always get written confirmation from the customer that they are, or are not, an end user. Without it, the default is to apply the reverse charge.

items.label: No written confirmation
items.detail: Default to the reverse charge if unconfirmed

scenes.heading: Module 16 summary
scenes.narration: To wrap up the module: business customers default to their own location as place of supply, consumers to the supplier's. Special rules cover some services, and reverse charges handle cross-border and construction cases.

items.label: Default place of supply
items.detail: B2B: customer's place. B2C: supplier's place

items.label: Special rules
items.detail: Land, transport, cultural, digital B2C

items.label: Reverse charge
items.detail: Cross-border B2B services received

items.label: CIS DRC
items.detail: VAT and CIS registered, customer not end user

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Remember these key points about the CIS domestic reverse charge before we talk it through together.

scenes.heading: VAT on Land and Property: The Default
scenes.subheading: Why land and buildings start out exempt, and what that means for costs
scenes.narration: Welcome to VAT on land and property. We start with the default treatment, because it shapes everything else in this module.

scenes.heading: Exempt by Default
scenes.narration: Supplies of land and buildings are exempt by default. The rule sits in Schedule 9, Group 1 of the VAT Act 1994.

items.label: Land and buildings
items.detail: The default VAT treatment

items.label: Legal source
items.detail: VAT Act, Schedule 9, Group 1

scenes.heading: The Cost of Exemption
scenes.narration: Here's the catch. Because the supply is exempt, the business cannot recover input VAT on the costs related to it, so that VAT becomes a real cost.

items.label: Input VAT blocked
items.detail: VAT on related costs cannot be reclaimed

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: land and buildings are exempt by default under Schedule 9, Group 1, and that exemption blocks recovery of input VAT on related costs.

scenes.heading: VAT on Residential Property
scenes.subheading: How VAT applies to selling, renting, building and working on homes
scenes.narration: In this section we look at residential property, where different transactions get very different VAT treatment. Getting this right matters, because the rate can range from zero to the full standard rate.

scenes.heading: Selling versus renting homes
scenes.narration: When a developer sells or grants a long lease on a new dwelling, it is zero-rated. Renting out residential property, on the other hand, is exempt.

items.label: Sale or long lease
items.detail: New dwelling sold or long-leased by the developer

items.label: Renting out
items.detail: Letting residential property

scenes.heading: Building and converting homes
scenes.narration: Constructing a new dwelling is zero-rated. Converting a non-residential building into residential use, or renovating a dwelling empty for at least two years, attracts the five percent reduced rate.

items.label: New dwelling construction
items.detail: Building a brand new home

items.label: Conversion to residential
items.detail: Non-residential building turned into homes

items.label: Empty dwelling renovation
items.detail: Dwelling vacant for 2 years or more

scenes.heading: Repairs are standard-rated
scenes.narration: Be careful with ordinary repairs and maintenance to dwellings. These do not get any relief and are charged at the standard rate of twenty percent.

items.label: Repairs and maintenance
items.detail: Standard rate applies to work on dwellings

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So, remember: new homes are zero-rated, renting is exempt, conversions and long-empty renovations are five percent, and repairs are twenty percent.

scenes.heading: VAT on Commercial Property
scenes.subheading: How sales, leases and construction are treated, with and without an option to tax
scenes.narration: In this section we look at commercial property. Whether a transaction is standard rated or exempt depends on what it is, and on whether an option to tax has been made.

scenes.heading: Always standard rated at 20%
scenes.narration: Two transactions are standard rated at 20% by default: selling a new commercial building under three years old, and constructing a new commercial building. An option to tax doesn't apply to either.

items.label: Sale of new commercial
items.detail: Under 3 years old; option to tax not applicable

items.label: Construction of new
items.detail: New commercial build; option to tax not applicable

scenes.heading: Old commercial: default vs OTT
scenes.narration: Selling an old commercial building, three years or older, and leasing commercial property are both exempt by default. If an option to tax is made, they become standard rated at 20%.

items.label: Default
items.detail: Sale of old commercial, 3+ years, and leases

items.label: If option to tax made
items.detail: Sale of old commercial and leases become standard

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: new commercial sales and construction are standard rated, while old commercial sales and leases are exempt unless an option to tax is made.

scenes.heading: The Option to Tax
scenes.subheading: Turning exempt commercial property into standard-rated supplies
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the option to tax, an election that changes how VAT applies to a specific commercial property or piece of land, and why landlords use it.

scenes.heading: What the election changes
scenes.narration: Without the option, supplies of the property are exempt. Once you opt, they become standard-rated, which unlocks recovery of input VAT on property costs.

items.label: Without the option
items.detail: No recovery of input VAT on property costs

items.label: With the option
items.detail: Input VAT on property costs can be recovered

scenes.heading: Key time limits
scenes.narration: Notify HM Revenue and Customs on form VAT1614A within 30 days. There is a six-month cooling-off period, then the option is locked in for 20 years, and it can be revoked after 20 years.

items.label: Notify on VAT1614A
items.detail: Tell HM Revenue and Customs of the election

items.label: Cooling-off period
items.detail: Window early on to reverse the election

items.label: Lock-in period
items.detail: The election binds the property

items.label: Revocation
items.detail: Option can be revoked after 20 years

scenes.heading: Impact on tenants
scenes.narration: Watch the tenant side. For partially-exempt or non-registered tenants, VAT on rent can't be recovered, so it's a real cost, and that reduces the rent a landlord can achieve.

items.label: Irrecoverable VAT on rent
items.detail: Insurance brokers, banks, charities bear the cost

items.label: Lower achievable rent
items.detail: Tenants factor the extra VAT into what they'll pay

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: opting makes the property standard-rated to recover input VAT, notify within 30 days, mind the time limits, and consider the tenants.

scenes.heading: Capital Goods Scheme: buildings
scenes.subheading: How VAT recovery on big property spends is monitored over time
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the Capital Goods Scheme for buildings. It matters because the VAT you recover on a large property spend isn't fixed on day one.

scenes.heading: When the scheme applies
scenes.narration: The scheme covers commercial buildings and refurbishments costing more than two hundred and fifty thousand pounds, excluding VAT. Recovery is then monitored over ten intervals.

items.label: Cost threshold
items.detail: Commercial buildings or refurbishments, excluding VAT

items.label: Monitoring period
items.detail: Input VAT recovery is monitored over 10 intervals

scenes.heading: Working out the annual adjustment
scenes.narration: If the taxable use percentage changes, you make an annual adjustment. Take one tenth of the total input VAT, then multiply by this year's taxable percentage minus the original year's.

items.label: Check taxable use
items.detail: Has the taxable use percentage changed this year?

items.label: Take one tenth
items.detail: Total input VAT × 1/10

items.label: Apply the change
items.detail: × (current year taxable% − original year taxable%)

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: buildings over two hundred and fifty thousand pounds, ten intervals, and an annual adjustment whenever taxable use changes, using one tenth of the total input VAT.

scenes.heading: Transfer of a Going Concern
scenes.subheading: When selling a business, or part of one, falls outside the scope of VAT
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the transfer of a going concern, often called TOGC. If the conditions are met, the sale of a business is outside the scope of VAT, so getting them right really matters.

scenes.heading: The four TOGC conditions
scenes.narration: All of these conditions must be met. The assets must be a business able to run separately, and the buyer must carry on the same kind of business, register for VAT where needed, and opt to tax property in time.

items.label: Separate operation
items.detail: Assets sold as a business capable of separate operation

items.label: Same kind of business
items.detail: Buyer uses the assets in the same kind of business

items.label: Buyer VAT-registered
items.detail: If seller is registered, buyer is or registers immediately

items.label: Opt to tax property
items.detail: Buyer opts to tax and notifies before the relevant date

scenes.heading: Module 17 recap
scenes.narration: To round off the module: property is exempt by default with many exceptions, the option to tax unlocks input recovery, the Capital Goods Scheme adjusts recovery, and TOGC can take a transfer outside VAT.

items.label: Exempt by default
items.detail: Property is exempt, with extensive exceptions

items.label: Option to tax
items.detail: Exempt commercial becomes standard; beware tenant impact

items.label: Capital Goods Scheme
items.detail: Adjusts input recovery for property over £250k

items.label: TOGC
items.detail: Takes a property transfer outside the scope of VAT

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Remember, every condition must be met for TOGC treatment, and for property the buyer's option to tax must be made and notified before the relevant date.

scenes.heading: The partial-exemption principle
scenes.subheading: Why mixed businesses cannot reclaim all their input VAT
scenes.narration: Welcome to partial exemption. When a business makes both taxable and exempt supplies, it cannot simply reclaim all the VAT it pays, so let's see why and how it is handled.

scenes.heading: Two types of supply
scenes.narration: A partly exempt business makes two kinds of supply: taxable supplies and exempt supplies. Because some of its activity is exempt, not all of its input VAT can be recovered.

items.label: Taxable supplies
items.detail: Part of the business's mixed activity

items.label: Exempt supplies
items.detail: Their presence limits input VAT recovery

scenes.heading: Working out recoverable VAT
scenes.narration: The method has two parts. First, input VAT is directly attributed where possible, then whatever remains, the residual, is apportioned.

items.label: Direct attribution
items.detail: Attribute input VAT directly where possible

items.label: Residual apportionment
items.detail: Apportion the remaining input VAT

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: mixed taxable and exempt supplies mean not all input VAT is recoverable, and the answer is direct attribution followed by residual apportionment.

scenes.heading: The Standard Method
scenes.subheading: How partially exempt businesses work out recoverable input VAT under Reg 101
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the standard method under regulation 101, the default way a partially exempt business works out how much input VAT it can recover.

scenes.heading: Step one: direct attribution
scenes.narration: First, every input is assigned to one of three pots: used for taxable supplies, used for exempt supplies, or residual, meaning it serves both.

items.label: Taxable
items.detail: Inputs used only to make taxable supplies

items.label: Exempt
items.detail: Inputs used only to make exempt supplies

items.label: Residual
items.detail: Inputs used for both, so must be apportioned

scenes.heading: The residual recovery percentage
scenes.narration: Divide taxable supplies by total supplies, both excluding VAT, and multiply by 100. Round up to the nearest whole percent, unless residual VAT is over £400k a month.

items.label: Taxable supplies
items.detail: Excluding VAT

items.label: Divide by total supplies
items.detail: Also excluding VAT, then multiply by 100

items.label: Round up
items.detail: To the nearest whole percent

scenes.heading: Exception to rounding up
scenes.narration: Watch the exception: rounding up to a whole percent does not apply where residual VAT is more than £400k a month.

items.label: No round-up above
items.detail: Residual VAT above this is not rounded up

scenes.heading: What the business recovers
scenes.narration: Finally, the business recovers all VAT directly attributable to taxable supplies, plus the residual VAT multiplied by the recovery percentage.

items.label: Directly taxable VAT
items.detail: Recovered in full

items.label: Plus residual share
items.detail: Residual VAT times the recovery percentage

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: attribute directly, calculate the percentage on supplies excluding VAT, round up unless above £400k a month, then add the two recoverable amounts.

scenes.heading: Partial Exemption: De Minimis
scenes.subheading: When small amounts of exempt input VAT can be recovered in full
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the de minimis test. If a business's exempt input VAT is small enough, it can recover all of it, which makes a real difference to cost.

scenes.heading: Working out exempt input VAT
scenes.narration: First, add together the input VAT directly linked to exempt supplies and the exempt share of residual input VAT. That total is what we test.

items.label: Direct exempt input VAT
items.detail: VAT directly attributable to exempt supplies

items.label: Share of residual VAT
items.detail: The exempt portion of residual input VAT

items.label: Total exempt input VAT
items.detail: Direct plus share of residual

scenes.heading: The two de minimis limits
scenes.narration: The test has two parts, and both must be met: exempt input VAT must average no more than six hundred and twenty-five pounds a month, and be no more than half of total input VAT.

items.label: Monthly average limit
items.detail: Exempt input VAT at or below this average

items.label: Share of total input VAT
items.detail: Exempt input VAT at or below half the total

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: total the direct and residual exempt VAT, check both limits, and if you pass, all of the exempt input VAT becomes recoverable.

scenes.heading: Partial Exemption: Annual Adjustment
scenes.subheading: Turning quarterly provisional recovery into a final full-year figure
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the annual adjustment, which makes sure the VAT you recover across the year is based on the real full-year figures, not just quarterly estimates.

scenes.heading: How the annual adjustment works
scenes.narration: Each quarter you recover using a provisional ratio. After the year ends, you recalculate using full-year figures and put the adjustment through on the next return.

items.label: Quarterly recovery
items.detail: Use provisional ratios each quarter

items.label: Recalculate at year-end
items.detail: Use the full-year figures

items.label: Adjust next return
items.detail: Enter the difference on the first return after year-end

scenes.heading: Worked Example 18.1: the figures
scenes.narration: Here's a business with taxable supplies of four hundred thousand pounds and exempt supplies of one hundred thousand. Its input VAT splits into directly taxable, directly exempt and residual amounts.

items.label: Taxable supplies
items.detail: Exempt supplies are £100k

items.label: Directly taxable input VAT
items.detail: Fully recoverable

items.label: Directly exempt input VAT
items.detail: Not recoverable

items.label: Residual input VAT
items.detail: Shared between taxable and exempt

scenes.heading: Working out recovery
scenes.narration: The recovery percentage is taxable over total supplies, so four hundred over five hundred, giving eighty percent. Recovery is thirty thousand plus eighty percent of twenty thousand, which is forty-six thousand pounds.

items.label: Recovery percentage
items.detail: £400k taxable ÷ £500k total supplies

items.label: VAT blocked
items.detail: £5k direct exempt + £4k of residual

scenes.heading: De minimis test: failed
scenes.narration: The de minimis limit for this three-month period is six hundred and twenty-five pounds times three, so one thousand eight hundred and seventy-five pounds. Nine thousand is well above that, so the test fails and nine thousand stays blocked.

items.label: De minimis limit
items.detail: £625 × 3 months

items.label: Exempt input VAT
items.detail: Exceeds the limit, so £9k remains blocked

scenes.heading: Module 18 key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: attribute directly, apportion residual by taxable over total, de minimis allows full recovery when exempt input VAT is small, and the annual adjustment reconciles the year's quarterly provisionals.

scenes.heading: VAT error correction thresholds
scenes.subheading: When to fix a VAT error on your next return and when to report it to HMRC
scenes.narration: Mistakes on VAT returns happen, and how you correct them depends on the size of the error. Let's look at the thresholds that decide which route you take.

scenes.heading: Errors you can fix on the next return
scenes.narration: A net error of ten thousand pounds or less is simply corrected on your next return. Errors above that, up to fifty thousand pounds or one percent of Box 6, whichever is greater, can also go on the next return.

items.label: Small net error
items.detail: Adjust Box 1 or Box 4 on the next return

items.label: Mid-size net error
items.detail: Or 1% of Box 6 if greater; still next return

scenes.heading: Next return or form VAT652?
scenes.narration: Once a net error goes above fifty thousand pounds or one percent of Box 6, it can't go on the next return. Instead you report it to HMRC on form VAT652.

items.label: Within the limit
items.detail: Up to £50k or 1% of Box 6, whichever is greater

items.label: Above the limit
items.detail: Over £50k or 1% of Box 6: report separately

scenes.heading: Deliberate errors
scenes.narration: Size doesn't matter for deliberate errors. Any error made on purpose must always be reported on form VAT652, never quietly adjusted on the next return.

items.label: Deliberate error, any size
items.detail: Always reported on form VAT652

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So, remember the thresholds: small errors go on the next return, larger ones on form VAT652, and deliberate errors always go on VAT652.

scenes.heading: Points-based VAT penalties
scenes.subheading: How the regime from January 2023 handles late returns and late payments
scenes.narration: Since January 2023, late VAT returns and late VAT payments are penalised under a new regime. Let's walk through how points, percentage penalties and interest work, so you can keep clients out of trouble.

scenes.heading: Late submission: penalty points
scenes.narration: Each missed submission deadline earns one point. Once points reach the threshold for the filing frequency, four for quarterly, five for monthly or two for annual, a £200 penalty applies, and another £200 for each later miss.

items.label: Quarterly threshold
items.detail: 1 point per missed deadline

items.label: Monthly threshold
items.detail: 1 point per missed deadline

items.label: Annual threshold
items.detail: 1 point per missed deadline

items.label: Penalty at threshold
items.detail: Plus £200 for each subsequent miss

scenes.heading: Late payment penalties
scenes.narration: For late payment, nothing is charged for the first fifteen days. From day sixteen to thirty it's 3%, and from day thirty-one it's 6% plus a daily penalty at 10% a year.

items.label: No penalty
items.detail: Nil if paid within 15 days

items.label: First penalty
items.detail: 3% penalty

items.label: Higher penalty
items.detail: 6% plus daily penalty at 10% per annum

scenes.heading: Late payment interest
scenes.narration: On top of penalties, late payment interest is charged at the Bank of England base rate plus 2.5%, running from the original due date.

items.label: Interest rate
items.detail: Bank of England base rate plus 2.5%

items.label: Charged from
items.detail: Interest runs from the payment due date

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: points for late returns, £200 penalties at the threshold, tiered penalties for late payment, and interest from the due date. Paying within fifteen days avoids a late payment penalty entirely.

scenes.heading: VAT inspections
scenes.subheading: How HMRC selects, what it reviews, and how to prepare your client
scenes.narration: In this section we look at VAT inspections: why HMRC picks a business, what the inspector checks, and how you as the practitioner should prepare and support your client.

scenes.heading: How HMRC selects businesses
scenes.narration: HMRC chooses businesses to inspect in three ways: based on their risk profile, through a random sample, or because of intelligence it has received. Typically you get about 7 days notice.

items.label: Risk profile
items.detail: Businesses flagged as higher risk

items.label: Random sample
items.detail: Any business can be picked at random

items.label: Intelligence
items.detail: Information received by HMRC

items.label: Notice period
items.detail: Typical notice before the visit

scenes.heading: What the inspector reviews
scenes.narration: The inspector reviews the VAT control account reconciliation, a sample of sales and purchase invoices, the treatment of cars, entertainment and property, and any apportionment workings.

scenes.heading: Practitioner preparation
scenes.narration: Before the visit, review the last 4 returns, identify any known issues first, and brief your client on what to say. Then always attend the inspection alongside your client.

items.label: Review last 4 returns
items.detail: Check recent VAT returns before the visit

items.label: Identify known issues
items.detail: Find any problems first, before HMRC does

items.label: Brief the client
items.detail: Agree what the client will say

items.label: Attend with the client
items.detail: Always be present at the inspection

scenes.heading: Module 19 key takeaways
scenes.narration: To wrap up the module: errors up to ten thousand pounds can go on the next return, larger or deliberate ones use form VAT652, late penalties are points based since January 2023, and inspections need active practitioner management.

scenes.heading: Making Tax Digital for VAT: Scope
scenes.subheading: Who must follow Making Tax Digital for VAT, and who may be exempt
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module 20. In this section we look at who Making Tax Digital for VAT applies to, so you can tell clients straight away whether the rules affect them.

scenes.heading: Who is in scope?
scenes.narration: From 1 April 2022, every VAT-registered business must comply, whatever its turnover. The only way out is a limited exemption for businesses that are digitally excluded.

items.label: All VAT-registered firms
items.detail: Must comply from 1 April 2022

items.label: Any turnover
items.detail: Turnover makes no difference to the rule

items.label: Digital exclusion
items.detail: Limited exemption available

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: from 1 April 2022, all VAT-registered businesses are in, regardless of turnover, and only digital exclusion gives a limited exemption.

scenes.heading: Digital records required
scenes.subheading: What Making Tax Digital for VAT expects you to keep in digital form
scenes.narration: In this section we look at exactly which records must be kept digitally under Making Tax Digital for VAT, so your client's returns are built on the right data.

scenes.heading: Business-level records
scenes.narration: First, the business's designatory data: its name, address, VAT registration number and any scheme it uses. Then any adjustments, such as those under the Flat Rate Scheme or for partial exemption.

items.label: Designatory data
items.detail: Name, address, VAT registration number, scheme

items.label: Adjustments
items.detail: For example Flat Rate Scheme, partial exemption

scenes.heading: Supplies made and received
scenes.narration: For every output supply, record its time, value and VAT rate. For every input supply, record its time, value and the VAT you can recover.

items.label: Each output supply
items.detail: Time, value and rate

items.label: Each input supply
items.detail: Time, value and VAT recoverable

scenes.heading: Retailers: Daily Gross Takings
scenes.narration: A shop using a retail scheme must also keep its Daily Gross Takings digitally, alongside its other records.

items.label: Shop uses retail scheme
items.detail: Sales are captured through the till

items.label: Records takings each day
items.detail: Daily Gross Takings kept in digital form

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: designatory data, adjustments, details of every output and input supply, and Daily Gross Takings for retail schemes must all be kept digitally.

scenes.heading: Digital links: the chain
scenes.subheading: How data must move between software under Making Tax Digital for VAT
scenes.narration: Under Making Tax Digital for VAT, your records have to flow through an unbroken chain of digital links. Let's look at what counts as a digital link, and what breaks the chain.

scenes.heading: Permitted digital links
scenes.narration: These all count as digital links: API connections, exporting and importing files such as CSV, XML, XLS or XLSX, linked cells in a workbook, and a file emailed and then imported.

items.label: API connections
items.detail: Software talks directly to software

items.label: File export and import
items.detail: CSV, XML, XLS or XLSX files

items.label: Linked cells
items.detail: Cells linked within a workbook

items.label: Emailed file, then imported
items.detail: The file is sent, then imported

scenes.heading: Not permitted: these break the chain
scenes.narration: Anything involving manual transfer is not allowed: re-typing data, copying and pasting values, or transcribing figures from printouts.

items.label: Re-typing
items.detail: Keying the data in again by hand

items.label: Copy-paste of values
items.detail: Pasting values rather than linking

items.label: Transcribing printouts
items.detail: Copying figures from paper

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: data must move digitally from start to finish. Links, imports and APIs are fine; any manual re-entry breaks the chain.

scenes.heading: Bridging software
scenes.subheading: How spreadsheet users can still submit VAT returns under Making Tax Digital
scenes.narration: In this section we look at bridging software, the tool that lets businesses keep using spreadsheets while still meeting Making Tax Digital for VAT.

scenes.heading: Examples of bridging software
scenes.narration: Bridging software is for spreadsheet users. Examples include Avalara, BX, VitalTax and Easy MTD VAT.

scenes.heading: How bridging works
scenes.narration: The software takes the nine boxes of the VAT return from your workbook, then submits them through the Making Tax Digital interface.

items.label: Prepare the workbook
items.detail: VAT figures are kept in a spreadsheet

items.label: Take the 9 boxes
items.detail: Software reads the nine VAT return boxes

items.label: Submit via MTD API
items.detail: Return is sent through the MTD interface

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: bridging software is for spreadsheet users, it takes the nine boxes from a workbook, and it submits them through the Making Tax Digital interface.

scenes.heading: Making Tax Digital for VAT: Penalties
scenes.subheading: What non-compliance costs, plus a recap of the whole module
scenes.narration: In this final section we look at what happens if a business doesn't follow Making Tax Digital for VAT, and then we'll recap the key points of the module.

scenes.heading: Penalties for non-MTD compliance
scenes.narration: A business that isn't compliant with Making Tax Digital can face a penalty of up to fifteen pounds a day. On top of that, the standard late penalty regime still applies.

items.label: Non-MTD compliance
items.detail: Daily penalty for failing to follow MTD rules

items.label: Late penalty regime
items.detail: Applies in addition to the daily penalty

scenes.heading: Module 20 recap
scenes.narration: Let's pull the module together. Every VAT-registered business is in scope, records must be digital, links must be digital throughout, and bridging software helps spreadsheet users.

items.label: Who is in scope
items.detail: All VAT-registered businesses

items.label: Digital records
items.detail: Designatory data, supplies and adjustments

items.label: Digital links
items.detail: Re-keying data breaks compliance

items.label: Bridging software
items.detail: Keeps spreadsheet users compliant

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Remember these points: the daily penalty, the late penalty regime on top, digital records, unbroken digital links, and bridging software for spreadsheets.

scenes.heading: PAYE in One Paragraph
scenes.subheading: How employers collect Income Tax and National Insurance for HMRC
scenes.narration: Welcome to PAYE, short for Pay As You Earn. It's the backbone of every payroll you'll run, so let's get the essentials clear before we dig into tax codes and reporting.

scenes.heading: How PAYE Works
scenes.narration: Under Pay As You Earn, the employer deducts Income Tax and National Insurance from employees' wages, then pays those amounts over to HMRC each month.

items.label: Deduct from wages
items.detail: Income Tax and National Insurance taken from pay

items.label: Pay HMRC monthly
items.detail: Employer passes the deductions to HMRC each month

scenes.heading: The Legal Basis
scenes.narration: PAYE rests on two pieces of law: the Income Tax PAYE Regulations 2003, and the Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992, which covers National Insurance.

items.label: Income Tax (PAYE) Regs
items.detail: Statutory instrument SI 2003/2682

items.label: Social Security Act
items.detail: Social Security Contributions & Benefits Act

scenes.heading: Real Time Information
scenes.narration: Since 2013, Real Time Information, known as RTI, has required employers to report each pay event to HMRC on or before the date the payment is made.

items.label: RTI introduced
items.detail: Real Time Information reporting begins

items.label: Report each pay event
items.detail: On or before the date payment is made

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: employers deduct tax and National Insurance, pay HMRC monthly, follow two key laws, and report every pay event under RTI no later than payday.

scenes.heading: Setting up a PAYE scheme
scenes.subheading: How employers register with HMRC and the references they receive
scenes.narration: Before you can pay staff through PAYE, the employer must register with HMRC. Let's look at how that works and the two references you'll need.

scenes.heading: Registering as an employer
scenes.narration: Registration is done online at gov dot uk forward slash register hyphen employer. HMRC then issues two references, so allow five working days for them to arrive.

items.label: Register online
items.detail: gov.uk/register-employer

items.label: HMRC issues references
items.detail: Employer PAYE and Accounts Office references

items.label: Allow time
items.detail: Allow 5 working days for issuance

scenes.heading: The two HMRC references
scenes.narration: The Employer PAYE reference looks like 123 slash AB45678. The Accounts Office reference has thirteen characters, such as 123PA00012345.

items.label: Employer PAYE reference
items.detail: Example format issued by HMRC

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Both references are needed for Real Time Information submissions and for employees' P60s and P45s, so register early and keep them safe.

items.label: Both appear on P60s and P45s

scenes.heading: Tax codes for 2024/25
scenes.subheading: How a tax code tells the employer an employee's tax-free pay
scenes.narration: A tax code tells the employer how much tax-free pay an employee gets. Read it wrongly and you deduct the wrong tax, so let's decode them properly.

scenes.heading: The standard code
scenes.narration: The standard code is 1257L, which gives the full personal allowance of twelve thousand, five hundred and seventy pounds.

items.label: Standard tax code
items.detail: L suffix means the standard personal allowance

items.label: Personal allowance
items.detail: Tax-free pay for the year

scenes.heading: Suffixes and prefixes
scenes.narration: M means the employee receives ten percent of their partner's allowance through Marriage Allowance, and N means they transfer ten percent of their own. T means adjustments, so call HM Revenue and Customs for details. A K prefix is a negative allowance.

items.label: M suffix
items.detail: Receives 10% of partner's PA: Marriage Allowance

items.label: N suffix
items.detail: Transfers 10% of own PA to partner

items.label: T suffix
items.detail: Includes adjustments; call HMRC if details needed

items.label: K prefix
items.detail: Negative allowance: add £4,750 to taxable pay a year

scenes.heading: Flat-rate and special codes
scenes.narration: Some codes apply one rate to all earnings: BR at twenty percent, usually a second job, D0 at forty and D1 at forty-five. NT means no tax, and 0T gives no allowance, for emergencies or a new starter without a P45.

items.label: All earnings taxed
items.detail: BR 20%, often 2nd job; D0 40%; D1 45%

items.label: Special codes
items.detail: NT no tax; 0T no PA, emergency or no P45

scenes.heading: Country prefixes
scenes.narration: An S prefix marks a Scottish taxpayer, so Scottish rates apply. A C prefix marks a Welsh taxpayer, though Welsh rates currently match English ones.

items.label: S prefix
items.detail: Scottish taxpayer: Scottish rates apply

items.label: C prefix
items.detail: Welsh taxpayer: rates currently match English

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Normally tax is cumulative, comparing cumulative pay with cumulative free pay. New starters or mid-year changes may go on Week 1 Month 1, non-cumulative, until HMRC's next P6 arrives.

items.label: M, N, T and K adjust pay
BR, D0, D1 tax all earnings

scenes.heading: National Insurance: categories and rates
scenes.subheading: Class 1 NI categories, thresholds for 2024/25 and employer changes for 2025/26
scenes.narration: In this section we look at Class 1 National Insurance for 2024 to 25, which is split between the employee, called primary, and the employer, called secondary. Getting the category right means the right NI is deducted.

scenes.heading: Standard and reduced employee rates
scenes.narration: Category A is the standard adult employee: 8% and 2% for the employee, 13.8% for the employer. Category C, over State Pension age, pays 0%, while J, deferring NI with multiple jobs, pays 2% and 2%. Both still cost the employer 13.8%.

items.label: A: Standard adult
items.detail: Employer pays 13.8%

items.label: C: Over State Pension age
items.detail: Employer pays 13.8%

items.label: J: Deferring, multiple jobs
items.detail: Employer pays 13.8%

scenes.heading: Employer relief up to the UEL
scenes.narration: For categories H, M, V and Z, the employer pays 0% up to the Upper Earnings Limit, known as the UEL. H, M and V employees pay 8% and 2%, while Z, under 21 and deferring, pays 2% and 2%.

items.label: H: Apprentice under 25
items.detail: Employer 0% up to UEL

items.label: M: Under 21
items.detail: Employer 0% up to UEL

items.label: V: Veteran, first civvy year
items.detail: First year of civilian work; employer 0% up to UEL

items.label: Z: Under 21 deferring
items.detail: Employer 0% up to UEL

scenes.heading: NI thresholds 2024/25
