scenes.heading: Statutory Payments: An Overview
scenes.subheading: Six payments employers make through payroll, and which ones they can recover
scenes.narration: In this section we meet the six statutory payments employers handle through payroll. Knowing the triggers, rates and recovery rules for 2024 to 2025 is essential for getting payroll right.

scenes.heading: Statutory Sick Pay
scenes.narration: Statutory Sick Pay, or SSP, starts when an employee is sick for four days or more. It pays £116.75 a week for up to 28 weeks, and employers cannot recover it.

items.label: Trigger
items.detail: Employee sick for at least four days

items.label: Recoverable
items.detail: Employer bears the full cost

scenes.heading: Pregnancy and Adoption Pay
scenes.narration: Statutory Maternity Pay and Statutory Adoption Pay follow the same pattern: six weeks at 90 percent of pay, then 33 weeks at £184.03, or 90 percent if that is lower.

items.label: SMP: pregnancy
items.detail: 6wks at 90% pay; 33wks at £184.03 or 90% if lower

items.label: SAP: adoption
items.detail: 6wks at 90% pay; 33wks at £184.03

scenes.heading: Partner, Shared and Bereavement Pay
scenes.narration: Statutory Paternity Pay is for a birth or adoption partner. Shared Parental Pay lasts up to 37 weeks, and Parental Bereavement Pay covers the loss of a child under 18, for two weeks.

items.label: SPP: partner
items.detail: £184.03 a week, or 90% of pay if lower

items.label: ShPP and SPBP
items.detail: ShPP up to 37wks; SPBP 2wks, both at £184.03

scenes.heading: Recovering the Cost
scenes.narration: Employers can recover 92 percent of SMP, SPP, ShPP, SAP and SPBP. Under Small Employers' Relief, if Class 1 National Insurance is £45,000 or less, they recover 103 percent.

items.label: Standard recovery
items.detail: SMP, SPP, ShPP, SAP and SPBP

items.label: Small Employers' Relief
items.detail: Class 1 National Insurance of £45k or less

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: Let's recap the key points before we explore each payment in more detail together.

scenes.heading: Statutory Sick Pay in Detail
scenes.subheading: Who qualifies, when SSP starts and how long it can last
scenes.narration: In this section we look at Statutory Sick Pay, or SSP, in detail. Getting eligibility and start dates right means employees are paid correctly from day one.

scenes.heading: Who Qualifies for SSP
scenes.narration: To qualify, average weekly earnings must be at least £123 a week, and the employee must be sick for four or more days in a row, counting non-working days too.

items.label: Average weekly earnings
items.detail: Per week, to be eligible for SSP

items.label: Days sick in a row
items.detail: Includes non-working days

scenes.heading: Waiting Days and Linking
scenes.narration: The first three days are waiting days, so no SSP is paid for them. The exception is when this sickness links to a previous SSP period within eight weeks.

items.label: Waiting days
items.detail: SSP is not paid for these days

items.label: Linked periods
items.detail: Link to earlier SSP period means no new waiting days

scenes.heading: Maximum SSP Entitlement
scenes.narration: SSP doesn't run forever. The most an employee can receive is twenty-eight weeks.

items.label: Maximum SSP period
items.detail: Upper limit on SSP payments

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: Let's recap: check earnings and the length of sickness, remember the three waiting days and the eight week linking rule, and cap SSP at twenty-eight weeks.

scenes.heading: Statutory Maternity Pay: the detail
scenes.subheading: Who qualifies, what evidence you need and how employers recover it
scenes.narration: In this section we look at Statutory Maternity Pay, or SMP. You'll learn who qualifies, what evidence the employee provides, and how much the employer can claim back.

scenes.heading: Eligibility tests
scenes.narration: There are two tests. The employee needs 26 weeks' continuous service ending with the 15th week before the expected week of childbirth, and average weekly earnings of at least £123 over an eight week period ending 15 weeks before that week.

items.label: Continuous service
items.detail: Ending with the 15th week before the EWC

items.label: Average weekly earnings
items.detail: In the 8 weeks ending 15 weeks before the EWC

scenes.heading: Evidence and recovery
scenes.narration: The MATB1 form from the midwife is the evidence of pregnancy. Employers normally recover 92% of SMP paid, rising to 103% for those entitled to Small Employers' Relief.

items.label: Evidence
items.detail: Provided by the midwife

items.label: Standard recovery
items.detail: Of SMP paid

items.label: Small Employers' Relief
items.detail: Recovery for qualifying small employers

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: two eligibility tests, the MATB1 as evidence, and recovery at 92% or 103% with Small Employers' Relief.

scenes.heading: Recovering Statutory Payments via EPS
scenes.subheading: How employers claim back statutory pay and reduce the PAYE bill
scenes.narration: In this section we look at how employers recover statutory payments through the Employer Payment Summary, or EPS, and why it matters for the amount paid to HMRC.

scenes.heading: From payroll to recovery
scenes.narration: Payroll software works out the statutory payment and shows it on the Full Payment Submission. The claim is then made monthly on the Employer Payment Summary, which reduces the PAYE bill.

items.label: Software calculates
items.detail: Payroll software works out the statutory payment

items.label: Shown on FPS
items.detail: Reported on the Full Payment Submission

items.label: Claim on EPS Box 11/12
items.detail: Recovery claimed monthly on the EPS

items.label: PAYE bill reduced
items.detail: Less is paid over to HMRC

scenes.heading: Recovery rates
scenes.narration: Family payments are recovered at 92 percent as standard, or 103 percent with Small Employers' Relief, for employers whose Class 1 National Insurance is £45,000 or less.

items.label: Standard recovery
items.detail: Family statutory payments

items.label: Small Employers' Relief
items.detail: Where Class 1 NI is £45k or less

scenes.heading: Module 22 key rules
scenes.narration: Remember, Statutory Sick Pay has not been recoverable since 2014. For Statutory Maternity Pay, the employee needs 26 weeks' service and average weekly earnings at or above the Lower Earnings Limit.

items.label: SSP not recoverable
items.detail: Statutory Sick Pay cannot be claimed back

items.label: SMP eligibility
items.detail: Service, plus average weekly earnings at least the LEL

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So, payroll software calculates, the EPS claims monthly, family payments recover at 92 or 103 percent, and Statutory Sick Pay is not recoverable.

scenes.heading: Auto-Enrolment: The Duty
scenes.subheading: What the Pensions Act 2008 requires of every employer
scenes.narration: Welcome to auto-enrolment. In this section we look at the core legal duty every employer has, and why getting it wrong can be very costly.

scenes.heading: What every employer must do
scenes.narration: Under the Pensions Act 2008, every employer must automatically enrol every eligible jobholder into a qualifying pension scheme. There are no exceptions for employers.

items.label: Pensions Act 2008
items.detail: The law that creates the duty

items.label: Identify eligible jobholders
items.detail: Every eligible jobholder must be covered

items.label: Auto-enrol them
items.detail: Into a qualifying pension scheme

scenes.heading: Penalties for failure
scenes.narration: If an employer fails, The Pensions Regulator can fine them. Fines start at a four hundred pound fixed penalty and can rise to as much as ten thousand pounds a day.

items.label: Fixed penalty
items.detail: Fine from The Pensions Regulator

items.label: Escalating penalty
items.detail: The maximum daily fine

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: the duty comes from the Pensions Act 2008, it applies to every employer, and The Pensions Regulator can fine heavily for failure.

scenes.heading: Auto-Enrolment: Worker Categories
scenes.subheading: How age and earnings decide what an employer must do for each worker
scenes.narration: Every worker falls into a category based on their age and earnings. Getting the category right tells you exactly what the employer must do, so let's work through each one.

scenes.heading: Eligible Jobholder
scenes.narration: An eligible jobholder is aged from 22 up to State Pension age and earns £10,000 or more a year. The employer must auto-enrol them.

items.label: Age
items.detail: From 22 up to State Pension age

items.label: Earnings
items.detail: £10,000 or more a year

items.label: Action
items.detail: Employer must automatically enrol them

scenes.heading: Non-Eligible Jobholders
scenes.narration: Non-eligible jobholders earn above the Lower Earnings Limit but under £10,000. All can opt in; for those aged 16 to 21 or State Pension age to 74, the employer must contribute if they do.

items.label: Aged 16–21 or SPA–74
items.detail: Above LEL, under £10,000. Employer must contribute

items.label: Aged 22 to SPA
items.detail: At or above LEL, under £10,000. Right to opt in

scenes.heading: Entitled Worker
scenes.narration: An entitled worker is aged 16 to 74 and earns at or below the Lower Earnings Limit. They have the right to join a scheme, but the employer does not have to contribute.

items.label: Earnings
items.detail: At or below the Lower Earnings Limit

items.label: Action
items.detail: No employer contribution required

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: check age and earnings, then match the action. Auto-enrol, opt in, or join, and know when the employer must contribute.

scenes.heading: Minimum contributions
scenes.subheading: How auto-enrolment pension contributions are worked out on qualifying earnings
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the minimum pension contributions under auto-enrolment, and how they are calculated on qualifying earnings. Getting this right keeps employers compliant and staff paid correctly.

scenes.heading: The key figures for 2024/25
scenes.narration: Qualifying earnings sit in a band from six thousand two hundred and forty pounds to fifty thousand two hundred and seventy pounds. The total minimum is eight percent: three percent from the employer and five from the employee, including tax relief.

items.label: Lower limit of band
items.detail: Qualifying earnings start here

items.label: Upper limit of band
items.detail: Qualifying earnings stop here

items.label: Employer minimum
items.detail: Paid by the employer

items.label: Employee minimum
items.detail: Includes tax relief; total minimum 8%

scenes.heading: Worked example: salary of £30,000
scenes.narration: For a thirty thousand pound salary, take off the six thousand two hundred and forty pound lower limit to get qualifying earnings of twenty three thousand seven hundred and sixty pounds. Eight percent of that is one thousand nine hundred pounds eighty.

items.label: Employer share at 3%
items.detail: Employer contribution

items.label: Employee share at 5%
items.detail: Employee contribution, incl. tax relief

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: work on qualifying earnings within the band, apply eight percent in total, and split it three percent employer and five percent employee.

scenes.heading: Cyclical compliance
scenes.subheading: Declaring compliance and re-enrolling staff on a three-yearly cycle
scenes.narration: Auto-enrolment isn't a one-off job. In this section we'll look at the cycle of declarations and re-enrolment that keeps an employer compliant year after year.

scenes.heading: Key periods to know
scenes.narration: The initial declaration of compliance is due within five months of the duties start date. Employers may also postpone auto-enrolment by up to three months.

items.label: Postponement allowed
items.detail: Employers may delay auto-enrolment

items.label: Initial declaration
items.detail: Due within 5 months of the duties start date

scenes.heading: The three-yearly cycle
scenes.narration: Every three years, staff who opted out must be re-enrolled. Then a fresh declaration of compliance is due within five months of each re-enrolment date.

items.label: Triennial re-enrolment
items.detail: Re-enrol staff who opted out, every three years

items.label: Re-declaration
items.detail: Within 5 months of each re-enrolment date

scenes.heading: Module 23 summary
scenes.narration: To recap the module: eligible jobholders are aged 22 to State Pension age earning at least ten thousand pounds a year. Total contributions are 8 percent of qualifying earnings, 3 from the employer and 5 from the employee.

items.label: Eligible earnings
items.detail: Aged 22 to State Pension age, per year

items.label: Total contribution
items.detail: Of qualifying earnings

items.label: Employer share
items.detail: Paid by the employer

items.label: Employee share
items.detail: Paid by the employee

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Keep these points in mind, and remember each re-declaration of compliance goes to The Pensions Regulator.

scenes.heading: What is a Benefit in Kind?
scenes.subheading: Non-cash perks from employment, and who pays tax and National Insurance on them
scenes.narration: Welcome! In this section we look at what a benefit in kind is. Getting this right matters, because these perks carry tax for the employee and National Insurance for the employer.

scenes.heading: Who Pays What?
scenes.narration: A benefit in kind is a non-cash benefit given by reason of employment. The employee is taxed on it under the Income Tax Earnings and Pensions Act 2003, while the employer pays Class 1A National Insurance.

items.label: Employee
items.detail: Taxable under ITEPA 2003

items.label: Employer
items.detail: Employer pays Class 1A National Insurance

scenes.heading: Class 1A NI Rates
scenes.narration: The Class 1A rate is 13.8 percent in 2024 to 25, rising to 15 percent from 2025 to 26, so check which tax year you are working in.

items.label: Rate in 2024/25
items.detail: Class 1A NI paid by the employer

items.label: Rate from 2025/26
items.detail: Higher rate applies from 2025/26

scenes.heading: Benefits That Escape Charge
scenes.narration: Not every benefit is caught. Trivial benefits of 50 pounds or under, and certain exempt benefits, escape the charge altogether.

items.label: Trivial benefits
items.detail: Escape the charge

items.label: Certain exempt benefits
items.detail: Also escape the charge

scenes.heading: Key Takeaways
scenes.narration: So remember: a benefit in kind is a non-cash employment perk, taxed on the employee, with Class 1A on the employer, unless it is trivial or exempt.

scenes.heading: Common Benefits in Kind
scenes.subheading: How the cash equivalent is worked out for the benefits you'll meet most
scenes.narration: In this section we look at the most common benefits in kind and how each one's cash equivalent is calculated, because that figure is what gets taxed and reported.

scenes.heading: Cars and fuel
scenes.narration: Both car benefits use the CO2-based appropriate percentage. For a company car, it's applied to the list price. For free fuel, it's applied to a fixed £27,800 for 2024 to 25.

items.label: Company car
items.detail: List price × CO2-based appropriate %

items.label: Free fuel for company car
items.detail: 2024/25 figure × CO2-based appropriate %

scenes.heading: Loans and accommodation
scenes.narration: A loan over £10,000 is taxed at HMRC's official rate of 2.25% less any interest paid. Accommodation uses the annual value, or rent if higher, plus an interest charge if it cost over £75k.

items.label: Beneficial loan threshold
items.detail: Loan × official rate, minus interest paid

items.label: HMRC official rate
items.detail: Applied to the loan balance

items.label: Accommodation cost trigger
items.detail: Annual value or rent if higher, plus interest

scenes.heading: Taxed at cost to employer
scenes.narration: For these three, it's simple: the cash equivalent is just what the employer paid for them.

items.label: Private medical insurance
items.detail: Cost to employer

items.label: Gym membership
items.detail: Cost to employer

items.label: Non-cash vouchers
items.detail: Cost to employer

scenes.heading: Trivial benefits
scenes.narration: A trivial benefit is exempt, but only if it's £50 or less, isn't cash and isn't contractual. All three conditions must be met.

items.label: Trivial benefit limit
items.detail: Not cash and not contractual, then exempt

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Let's recap the cash equivalent rules before we dig into each one together.

scenes.heading: Payrolling vs P11D
scenes.subheading: Two ways to report benefits in kind and settle the tax and Class 1A NI due
scenes.narration: In this section we compare the two ways of reporting benefits in kind: filing P11D forms after the year ends, or payrolling benefits so tax is collected as you go.

scenes.heading: The P11D route
scenes.narration: Under the P11D route, you file a P11D for each employee and a P11D(b) for total Class 1A National Insurance by 6 July, then pay the Class 1A by 22 July.

items.label: File P11D per employee
items.detail: One form for each employee with benefits

items.label: File P11D(b)
items.detail: Shows total Class 1A National Insurance

items.label: Pay Class 1A NI
items.detail: Payment of the Class 1A due

scenes.heading: Payrolling benefits
scenes.narration: To payroll benefits, you register before the tax year starts, then tax is collected through PAYE in real time. You still file a P11D(b) for Class 1A.

items.label: Register in advance
items.detail: Before the start of the tax year

items.label: Tax through PAYE
items.detail: Collected in real time through payroll

items.label: Still file P11D(b)
items.detail: Needed to report Class 1A NI

scenes.heading: Payrolling becomes mandatory
scenes.narration: Payrolling becomes mandatory from April 2026 for most benefits in kind, so it's worth understanding now.

items.label: Mandatory payrolling
items.detail: Applies to most benefits in kind

scenes.heading: Key takeaways
scenes.narration: Remember these key dates and rules, and that the P11D(b) is needed under both methods.
